subject: Git & Version Control
summary: Git is the substrate every other DevOps tool sits on: CI triggers off refs, GitOps reconciles a cluster against a commit, releases are tags, and post-incident forensics is history archaeology. Interviewers probe it because almost everyone can commit and push, while very few can explain what a commit actually is, recover a repository after a bad force-push, resolve a genuine conflict without guessing, or design a branching and review policy that still works with two hundred engineers merging into one trunk. This subject builds from the object model upward - blobs, trees, commits, refs, the index - because nearly every confusing Git behaviour is an obvious consequence of that model once you can see it. From there it covers the operations that separate confident engineers from cargo-cultists: merge versus rebase and the history policy behind the choice, interactive rebase, cherry-pick and the merge-revert trap, reflog recovery, bisect automation, hooks and where enforcement actually belongs, submodules, monorepo scaling, secret removal, and the branching and PR practices that keep integration cheap.

sections.title: 1. The Object Model: Git Is a Content-Addressed Store
sections.content:
Almost every confusing thing about Git stops being confusing once you accept one fact: Git is not a system that records changes to files. It is a key-value store of immutable objects, where the key is the cryptographic hash of the value, plus a thin layer of pointers on top. Diffs, patches, and "changes" are computed on demand when you ask for them. They are not what is stored.

There are exactly four object types. A **blob** holds the raw bytes of a file — just the bytes. It does not know the file's name, its permissions, or when it was written. A **tree** is a directory listing: a sorted list of entries, each entry being a mode, a name, and the object ID of a blob (a file) or another tree (a subdirectory). A **commit** points at exactly one tree — the complete snapshot of the project at that moment — plus zero or more parent commits, an author, a committer, and a message. An **annotated tag** object points at another object (usually a commit) and carries a tagger, a message, and optionally a signature.

Every object is stored the same way. Git builds a header consisting of the type name, a space, the content length in bytes, and a NUL byte, prepends it to the content, and hashes the whole thing with SHA-1. That hash is the object's name. Then the header-plus-content is zlib-compressed and written to `.git/objects/ab/cdef...` where `ab` is the first two hex digits. You can reproduce Git's hashing by hand in one shell pipeline, which is the single best way to convince yourself there is no magic.

Three consequences follow, and interviewers probe all three.

**Deduplication is free and automatic.** Two identical files in different directories are one blob. A file that is unchanged across a thousand commits is one blob referenced by a thousand trees. This is why a repository with long history is not proportionally huge, and why Git stores full snapshots per commit without exploding — the snapshot is a tree of pointers, and unchanged subtrees are shared by identity.

**Git does not track renames; it detects them.** Because a blob has no name, moving `src/a.py` to `lib/a.py` creates no new blob at all. It creates new tree objects for the two affected directories and their ancestors, and a new commit. When you later run `git log --follow` or `git diff -M`, Git compares the deleted and added paths by content similarity and *infers* the rename after the fact. That is why rename detection has a similarity threshold (`-M50%` by default for most commands) and why a rename combined with a heavy edit shows up as delete + add.

**Commit IDs are transitive over all of history.** A commit's hash covers its tree hash and its parent hashes. Its parent's hash covers *its* tree and parents. So a commit ID is a checksum of the entire reachable history behind it. This is why you cannot quietly edit an old commit: change one byte in a commit from last March and every descendant commit gets a new ID. It is also why rebasing produces new commits rather than modifying old ones, why signed tags are meaningful (signing one commit attests to everything behind it), and why Git is tamper-evident by construction.

A word on SHA-1. The SHAttered attack in 2017 produced a real SHA-1 collision, so Git switched its default hashing to a hardened variant (`sha1dc`, since Git 2.13) that detects the specific bit patterns used in known collision-construction techniques and errors out instead of hashing. Git also gained support for SHA-256 repositories (`git init --object-format=sha256`), but that remains largely experimental and SHA-256 repos cannot interoperate with SHA-1 repos, so essentially every repository you will touch in an interview or at work is still SHA-1. The honest interview answer is: the collision risk is a supply-chain concern rather than an integrity-of-my-daily-work concern, the hardened hash mitigates the known attacks, and the migration path exists but is not widely deployed.

sections.title: 2. Refs, HEAD, and the Reachability Rule
sections.content:
If objects are the nouns, refs are the pronouns. A ref is a human-readable name for an object ID, and it is stored as literally that: a file under `.git/refs/` containing forty hex characters and a newline. `.git/refs/heads/main` is the branch `main`. `.git/refs/tags/v1.4.0` is a tag. `.git/refs/remotes/origin/main` is your last-known position of `main` on the remote. Once a repository accumulates many refs, Git compacts them into a single `.git/packed-refs` file for speed, and newer Git versions can use a `reftable` backend, but the model is unchanged: a name maps to an object ID.

This is the answer to "why is branching cheap in Git?" Creating a branch writes 41 bytes. It copies nothing, and it is O(1) regardless of repository size. A branch is not a container of commits — it is a movable label on one commit. The commits "on" a branch are simply the commits reachable from that label by walking parent pointers. Two branches that share history share it by pointing into the same object graph, not by duplicating it.

**HEAD** is one level of indirection above that. Normally `.git/HEAD` contains the text `ref: refs/heads/main` — a symbolic ref. That indirection is what makes committing work: `git commit` writes a new commit object whose parent is the current HEAD commit, then updates *whatever ref HEAD points at* to the new commit. The branch advances because HEAD is attached to it. When you check out a raw commit, a tag, or `origin/main`, Git writes the object ID directly into `.git/HEAD` instead. That is **detached HEAD**: you have a working tree and you can commit, but no branch label is following you, so as soon as you check out something else the commits you made become unreachable from any ref and are only findable through the reflog. Detached HEAD is not an error state — CI systems and `git bisect` deliberately operate detached — but it is a state where new work is one careless checkout away from being invisible.

Beyond branches and tags there is a small zoo of special refs and pseudo-refs, and knowing them separates people who have debugged Git from people who have only used it. `ORIG_HEAD` is written by merge, rebase, reset, and pull before they move HEAD — it is the one-step undo button. `FETCH_HEAD` records what the last fetch brought down. `MERGE_HEAD`, `REBASE_HEAD`, `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, and `REVERT_HEAD` exist only while the corresponding operation is in progress and are how Git knows it is mid-conflict. `refs/stash` holds the stash stack. Hosting platforms add their own: GitHub exposes pull requests as `refs/pull/<n>/head` and `refs/pull/<n>/merge`, GitLab as `refs/merge-requests/<n>/head`. Those platform refs matter operationally, because a commit you "deleted" by force-pushing can still be reachable through them.

The rule that ties objects and refs together is **reachability**, and it governs garbage collection. An object is safe if it is reachable from any ref, from the index, or from a reflog entry that has not yet expired. Everything else is garbage and will eventually be pruned. That single rule explains a family of otherwise mysterious behaviours: why a commit you "lost" by resetting is still recoverable (the reflog still names it); why it stops being recoverable after ninety days (reflog expiry); why `git gc` right after `git reflog expire --expire=now --all` genuinely destroys data; and why a blob containing a leaked secret can survive long after you deleted the branch it lived on.

Finally, learn the revision syntax properly, because interviewers use it as a quick competence check. `^` selects a *parent by number*: `HEAD^` is the first parent, `HEAD^2` is the second parent (only meaningful on a merge commit). `~` walks *generations along first parents*: `HEAD~2` is the grandparent via first parents, identical to `HEAD^^`. `A..B` means commits reachable from B but not A — the classic "what is on my branch that is not upstream". `A...B` (three dots) is the symmetric difference, the commits unique to either side, and paired with `--left-right` it is how you compute ahead/behind counts.

# Refs are files ----------------------------------------------------------
cat .git/HEAD                       # ref: refs/heads/main
cat .git/refs/heads/main            # 4a2f0b1c... (or look in .git/packed-refs)
git symbolic-ref HEAD               # refs/heads/main
git rev-parse HEAD                  # resolve to an object id
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD     # main
git update-ref refs/heads/rescue 4a2f0b1c   # create a branch with plumbing

# List everything, including the refs you forgot exist
git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate \
  --format='%(refname) %(objectname:short) %(committerdate:relative)'

# Revision syntax you must be able to read --------------------------------
HEAD^      # first parent
HEAD^2     # SECOND parent - only exists on a merge commit
HEAD~3     # three generations back, following first parents (== HEAD^^^)
main@{u}   # the upstream of main, e.g. origin/main
@{-1}      # the previously checked-out branch  (git switch - uses this)
HEAD@{2}   # reflog: where HEAD pointed two moves ago  (NOT an ancestor)
:/retry    # most recent commit whose message contains "retry"
main^{tree}  # the tree object of main's commit

# Ranges ------------------------------------------------------------------
git log origin/main..HEAD          # my unpushed commits
git log HEAD..origin/main          # commits I have not pulled yet
git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD   # "3  2" = behind 3, ahead 2

# Which refs can still reach this commit? (is it really orphaned?)
git branch --contains 4a2f0b1c
git tag --contains 4a2f0b1c
git for-each-ref --contains 4a2f0b1c

sections.title: 3. The Three Trees: Working Tree, Index, and HEAD
sections.content:
Git's command surface looks arbitrary until you see that almost every command is moving data between three places. **HEAD** is the commit you are on — the last committed snapshot. The **index** (also called the staging area or the cache) is a proposed next snapshot. The **working tree** is the actual files on disk. `git status` is a report of two diffs: HEAD-versus-index ("changes to be committed") and index-versus-working-tree ("changes not staged for commit").

The index deserves more attention than it usually gets, because it is not a list of diffs — it is a full, flat manifest. `.git/index` is a binary file holding one sorted entry per tracked path, and each entry contains the path, the file mode, the blob ID of the staged content, and a cache of the file's stat data from the last time Git looked at it: device, inode, ctime, mtime, size, uid, gid. When you `git add` a file, Git writes a blob into the object database immediately and records its ID in the index. The content is already durable in `.git/objects` at that point — which is exactly why `git fsck` can sometimes recover work you staged but never committed.

That stat cache is also the reason `git status` is normally instant. Git does not hash your files to see if they changed; it `lstat`s them and compares size and mtime against the cached values, and only hashes when the stat data differs. It also explains the failure modes: on a repository with hundreds of thousands of files, that is hundreds of thousands of syscalls, which is why large-monorepo tuning is mostly about avoiding them (`core.untrackedCache`, the built-in filesystem monitor `core.fsmonitor`, and sparse indexes). It explains why a filesystem with coarse timestamp granularity or a container bind-mount with skewed clocks can make Git see phantom modifications. And it is the mechanism behind `git update-index --assume-unchanged` and `--skip-worktree`, two flags people reach for to hide a locally-edited config file and then spend an afternoon wondering why their change will not push.

With the three trees in mind, the reset/checkout/restore family becomes a table rather than a mystery. `git reset` moves the current branch pointer and optionally updates the index and working tree; `git checkout`/`git switch`/`git restore` move HEAD or copy file contents but do not rewrite branch pointers in the same way.

- `git reset --soft <commit>`: moves the branch pointer only. Index and working tree untouched. Your changes are now staged relative to the new HEAD. This is the "uncommit but keep everything staged" move, and the basis of squashing the last N commits by hand.
- `git reset --mixed <commit>` (the default): moves the branch pointer and resets the index to match. Working tree untouched. This is "uncommit and unstage" — nothing on disk is lost.
- `git reset --hard <commit>`: moves the branch pointer, resets the index, and overwrites the working tree. This is the only variant that can destroy uncommitted work, and it does so silently.
- `git reset <paths>` with no `--flag`: does not move HEAD at all. It copies the given paths from HEAD into the index — i.e. unstage. Modern spelling: `git restore --staged <paths>`.
- `git restore <paths>`: copies from the index into the working tree — discard unstaged edits. `git restore --source=HEAD~2 <path>` pulls an old version into the working tree.

Git 2.23 split the overloaded `git checkout` into `git switch` (change branches) and `git restore` (restore file contents), and you should use them in an interview because the split demonstrates you understand that the old command was doing two unrelated jobs. The classic footgun it fixes: `git checkout <branch>` switches branches, but `git checkout <file>` throws away your edits to that file, with no confirmation and no reflog entry — and if the names collide, Git picks the branch.

One more thing the index does that most people never see: during a conflicted merge it holds up to three versions of the same path, called stages. Stage 1 is the merge base, stage 2 is "ours", stage 3 is "theirs". `git ls-files -u` shows them. This is not trivia — it is how `git checkout --ours <file>` knows what to give you, and why a file is considered "resolved" only when you `git add` it, collapsing three staged entries back to one.

sections.title: 4. Branching: Cheap Pointers, Expensive Divergence
sections.content:
Because a branch is 41 bytes, the cost of branching in Git is zero and the cost of *branch divergence* is everything. Interviewers who ask about branching are almost never asking about `git switch -c`; they are asking whether you understand what happens to a team when branches live for three weeks.

Mechanically, `git switch -c feature/x` writes `refs/heads/feature/x` pointing at the current commit and repoints HEAD at it. Nothing is copied. Committing on it advances only that ref. `git branch -d` refuses to delete a branch whose tip is not reachable from HEAD or its upstream; `git branch -D` deletes regardless. That reachability check is why `git branch --merged` gives the wrong answer under a squash-merge workflow: when a PR is squash-merged, main gets a *new* commit with the same content but a different ID, so your branch's actual commits are never reachable from main and Git honestly reports the branch as unmerged even though its content shipped. Teams that squash-merge should rely on the hosting platform's PR state (or `git cherry`, which compares by patch content) rather than on `--merged`.

Branch tracking is a separate mechanism from branch existence. `branch.<name>.remote` and `branch.<name>.merge` in `.git/config` record the upstream, which is what makes `git status` say "ahead 2, behind 3", what makes bare `git push` and `git pull` know where to go, and what `@{u}` resolves to. `git push -u origin HEAD` sets it on first push. A branch with no upstream is not broken, it just makes Git ask you for the destination every time.

The substantive part is divergence. When you branch off main and both sides move, the two histories share a merge base and then differ. Three costs grow with the age of that branch, and they do not grow linearly.

**Textual conflicts grow with the amount of overlapping change.** Two people editing the same function on the same day conflict trivially. Two people editing the same subsystem over three weeks conflict in a dozen places at once, at a moment when neither remembers the reasoning behind their own edits from week one.

**Semantic conflicts grow faster and are invisible to Git.** Git merges text. If your branch adds a call to `sendEmail(user)` while main changes that function's signature to `sendEmail(user, template)`, the merge is textually clean and the build is broken. No conflict markers, no warning. This class of failure is why "my branch is green and main is green" is not a guarantee, and it is the entire justification for merge queues (covered later).

**Rebase pain compounds.** Rebasing a 40-commit branch onto three weeks of main means replaying 40 patches, each of which can conflict, and resolving the same conflict repeatedly as it appears in commit after commit. That is the pain `git rerere` exists to soften, and it is also a signal you should have merged sooner.

The practical guidance interviewers want to hear is a policy, not a preference: keep branches short-lived (hours to a couple of days), integrate with main daily rather than at the end, split large work into independently shippable pieces behind a flag, and treat a branch that is a week old as a risk item rather than a normal state. Naming conventions (`feat/`, `fix/`, `<ticket-id>-short-slug`) matter less than lifetime, though they do help tooling route CI and CODEOWNERS.

Two more mechanics worth knowing. **Orphan branches** (`git switch --orphan gh-pages`) start with no parent and no history — useful for documentation sites or generated artefacts that share a repository but not a lineage. And **worktrees** (`git worktree add ../hotfix -b hotfix origin/main`) give you a second checked-out branch in a second directory backed by the same object database, which is a far better answer to "I need to fix prod while my feature build is warm" than stashing.

# Create, track, inspect --------------------------------------------------
git switch -c feat/rate-limit                # create + switch (modern)
git switch -                                 # back to previous branch (@{-1})
git push -u origin HEAD                      # push and set upstream
git branch -vv                               # local branches + upstream + ahead/behind

# Ahead/behind without guessing -------------------------------------------
git fetch origin
git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD    # "behind  ahead"

# Deleting safely ---------------------------------------------------------
git branch -d feat/old        # refuses unless merged (by reachability)
git branch -D feat/old        # force
git push origin --delete feat/old
git fetch --prune             # drop remote-tracking refs for deleted remotes
# make it automatic:
git config --global fetch.prune true

# Squash-merge blind spot -------------------------------------------------
git branch --merged main      # will NOT list squash-merged branches
git cherry -v main feat/x     # compares by PATCH; "-" prefix = already in main

# Housekeeping: list branches that are fully contained in main, by patch
for b in $(git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads/); do
  [ "$b" = main ] && continue
  [ -z "$(git cherry main "$b" | grep '^\+')" ] && echo "merged-by-content: $b"
done

# Parallel checkouts instead of stashing ----------------------------------
git worktree add ../hotfix -b hotfix origin/main
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../hotfix

sections.title: 5. Merging: Three-Way Merge, Merge Bases, and What ort Actually Does
sections.content:
A merge answers the question: given two versions of the project that diverged, what is the combined version? A naive two-way diff cannot answer it, because if your line says `timeout = 30` and mine says `timeout = 60`, two-way comparison cannot tell who changed and who kept. The missing ingredient is the **merge base**: the best common ancestor of the two commits. With base, ours, and theirs you can reason per-hunk — if only one side differs from the base, take that side; if both differ and they differ from each other, that is a conflict.

Finding the merge base is a graph problem: `git merge-base A B` returns the lowest common ancestor. Two subtleties matter. First, there can be more than one — a "criss-cross" history, produced when two branches merge each other in both directions, has multiple equally-good ancestors. Second, what Git does about that is the reason the default strategy is called *recursive* (historically) or *ort* (today): when there are multiple merge bases, Git recursively merges the bases together into a synthetic virtual base and uses that as the reference for the real merge. This produces better results than arbitrarily picking one base, and it is a genuinely good interview answer to the question "what does the recursive strategy do that a naive three-way merge does not?"

`ort` ("Ostensibly Recursive's Twin") replaced `recursive` as the default two-head merge strategy in Git 2.34. It is a from-scratch reimplementation that works on in-memory tree structures rather than repeatedly rewriting the on-disk index, which makes it dramatically faster on large repositories and on rebases with many steps, and it fixed a batch of long-standing rename-detection and directory-rename corner cases. For interview purposes: same conceptual algorithm, much better implementation, and it is what runs by default today.

**Fast-forward** is the degenerate case. If the merge base of your branch and the branch you are merging *is* your current commit — you have not moved since branching — there is nothing to merge. Git just slides the branch pointer forward. No merge commit is created, and history stays linear. `git merge --no-ff` forces a merge commit anyway, which teams use to preserve the fact that a group of commits belonged to one feature. `git merge --ff-only` refuses to merge unless it can fast-forward, which is the safety setting you want for `git pull` so it never silently creates a merge commit behind your back.

A real merge writes a commit with two or more parents. The **first parent is the branch you were on** when you ran the merge, the second is what you merged in. That ordering is load-bearing: `git log --first-parent` on main then shows you one entry per integration rather than every commit from every feature branch, which is how you get a readable release history out of a merge-based workflow. It is also why `git revert -m 1 <merge>` means "keep the mainline, undo what came in from the side branch".

Strategy options are worth distinguishing precisely, because candidates routinely conflate them. `-X ours` and `-X theirs` are *options to the ort strategy*: perform a normal merge, but for hunks that genuinely conflict, silently take one side instead of stopping. `-s ours` is a *different strategy entirely*: produce a merge commit whose tree is identical to the current branch, completely discarding the other side's content while still recording it as merged. `-s ours` has one legitimate use — recording that a branch has been superseded so it stops showing up as unmerged — and using it by accident silently deletes work. `-s octopus` merges more than two heads at once and is the default when you pass multiple branches, but it refuses to run if there are any conflicts.

Finally, the failure mode Git cannot protect you from: a **clean merge that breaks the build**. Git's merge is textual and structural, not semantic. Renames are detected by content similarity, and directory renames are inferred heuristically, but nothing checks that the merged code compiles or that the merged config is valid. The only real defences are short-lived branches (less divergence), a merge queue that builds and tests the *merged result* before it lands, and treating "green on my branch" as necessary but not sufficient.

# Inspect before you merge ------------------------------------------------
git merge-base main feat/x                 # the common ancestor
git merge-base --all main feat/x           # multiple = criss-cross history
git log --oneline $(git merge-base main feat/x)..feat/x     # what is coming in
git diff main...feat/x                     # 3-dot diff = changes on feat/x ONLY
                                           # (diffed against the merge base)

# Merge variants ----------------------------------------------------------
git merge --ff-only origin/main            # refuse to create a merge commit
git merge --no-ff feat/x                   # always create one (preserve grouping)
git merge --no-commit feat/x               # stage the result, let me inspect first
git merge --abort                          # bail out of a conflicted merge

# Strategy vs strategy-option (very different things) ---------------------
git merge -X ours feat/x    # normal merge; CONFLICTING hunks resolve to ours
git merge -X theirs feat/x  # normal merge; CONFLICTING hunks resolve to theirs
git merge -s ours feat/x    # tree = exactly current branch; feat/x content DISCARDED
                            # but recorded as merged. Use only to retire a branch.

# Readable history on a merge-based main ----------------------------------
git log --first-parent --oneline main      # one line per integration
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all

# Make pull safe by default -----------------------------------------------
git config --global pull.ff only
# then integrate deliberately: git pull --rebase   or   git merge origin/main

sections.title: 6. Rebase: Replaying Commits and Why the IDs Change
sections.content:
Rebase answers a different question from merge: instead of "combine two histories", it asks "what would my work look like if I had started from a newer base?" The mechanism is replay. Git computes the set of commits that are on your branch but not on the upstream — the range `upstream..HEAD` — then checks out the new base and re-applies each of those commits in order, one at a time.

Each replay is itself a small merge. For each commit being replayed, Git performs a three-way merge using that commit's parent as the base, the commit itself as one side, and the new base as the other. That is why a rebase can conflict once per replayed commit, and why the conflicts you resolve during a rebase are often the *same* conflict appearing again and again as each successive patch lands on the same modified region. (This is precisely what `git rerere` is for.)

The crucial consequence: **the replayed commits are new objects with new IDs**. A commit's hash covers its parent, and the parent changed, so the hash must change. Git preserves the original author name and *author date* but sets a fresh *committer* identity and committer date — the difference between those two fields is a durable fingerprint of a rebase, and `git log --format='%h %an %ad %cn %cd'` will show it. The old commits are not modified and not deleted; they simply become unreferenced by your branch and survive in the reflog until it expires.

Since Git 2.26 the default rebase engine is the **merge backend** (the same machinery as `git rebase -i`), replacing the old `am` backend which worked by generating text patches with `format-patch` and applying them with `git am`. The merge backend handles renames, mode changes, and binary files correctly; the patch backend often could not. `--apply` forces the old behaviour, and the only common reason to want it is speed on very long, simple rebases.

Two behaviours surprise people. First, rebase **silently drops commits that are already upstream**. It compares by patch-id — a hash of the diff, insensitive to line numbers and whitespace context — so if your commit was cherry-picked into main earlier, rebasing will notice the equivalent patch is already there and skip it rather than producing an empty commit or a conflict. This is usually what you want and occasionally deeply confusing. Second, by default rebase **flattens merge commits** out of the replayed range: a topic branch containing internal merges comes out linear. `--rebase-merges` preserves that topology by rebuilding it with `label`/`reset`/`merge` instructions in the todo list. (Its predecessor `--preserve-merges` was deprecated in favour of it and later removed.)

`git rebase --onto` is the form that solves problems nothing else solves, and it is worth memorising the argument order: `git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch>`. It means "take the commits in `upstream..branch` and replay them onto `newbase`". The classic uses are transplanting a branch that was accidentally started from the wrong parent, and cutting a stacked branch loose when the branch beneath it was squash-merged and its commits no longer exist upstream.

Modern quality-of-life options matter in practice. `--autostash` (or `rebase.autoStash=true`) stashes dirty working-tree changes, rebases, and restores them, instead of refusing to start. `--update-refs` (Git 2.38+, or `rebase.updateRefs=true`) is the feature that makes stacked branches usable: when you rebase the top of a stack, any other local branches pointing at commits inside the rebased range are moved along with them, instead of being left pointing at the pre-rebase copies.

The golden rule — *do not rebase commits that others have based work on* — is usually stated as etiquette, but the reason is mechanical. If you rewrite commits that someone else has pulled, their branch still contains the originals. When they next integrate, Git sees two lineages containing the same logical changes with different IDs, and the "fix" they instinctively reach for (`git pull`) merges the old copies back in, producing duplicated commits and a tangled graph. The rule is therefore not that rebasing is dangerous, but that rebasing is a local-history operation: once history is shared, you may only append to it, or coordinate an explicit rewrite with everyone who has a copy.
sections.code:
# Basic: replay my branch on top of the latest main -----------------------
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# conflict? resolve files, then:
git add <resolved-files>
git rebase --continue
# or: git rebase --skip     (drop this commit)
#     git rebase --abort    (restore the pre-rebase state exactly)
#     git rebase --quit     (stop, but KEEP the commits applied so far)

# --onto: the argument order is (newbase, upstream, branch) ---------------
#   before:   main ---A---B---C            feature/base
#                          \
#                           D---E---F      feature/top
#   goal: move D,E,F onto main, dropping A,B,C from their ancestry
git rebase --onto main feature/base feature/top

# Branch started from the wrong parent ------------------------------------
git rebase --onto main wrong-parent my-branch

# The whole stack at once (Git 2.38+) -------------------------------------
git rebase --update-refs origin/main       # moves every local branch inside the range
git config --global rebase.updateRefs true

# Quality of life ---------------------------------------------------------
git config --global rebase.autoStash true
git config --global rerere.enabled true    # remember conflict resolutions
git config --global pull.rebase true       # git pull == fetch + rebase

# Detect a rebase after the fact: author date != committer date -----------
git log --format='%h  A:%ad  C:%cd  %s' --date=short -5

# Preserve internal merge topology ----------------------------------------
git rebase --rebase-merges origin/main

# Recover from a rebase that went wrong (before reflog expiry) ------------
git reflog                                 # find the pre-rebase HEAD
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD                 # rebase sets ORIG_HEAD for you

sections.title: 7. Merge vs Rebase: Choosing a History Policy, Not a Side
sections.content:
The worst answer to "merge or rebase?" is a preference. The strong answer is: it depends on whether the history is shared yet, and beyond that it is a *team policy* that should be enforced by tooling rather than argued about per PR. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can reason about history as a product with consumers — bisect, blame, revert, release notes, incident forensics — rather than as an aesthetic.

Start with the invariant that is not negotiable: **rebase private history, merge public history.** Commits nobody else has are yours to reshape. Commits that exist on a shared branch must only be appended to, because rewriting them forces every other clone to reconcile two versions of the same work. Everything else is policy.

There are three policies in common use, and each is coherent.

**Merge commits (no-ff).** Every PR lands as a merge commit; the feature's individual commits are preserved verbatim. Pros: the true history is recorded, nothing is rewritten, and `git log --first-parent main` gives a clean one-line-per-feature view. Cons: the raw graph is noisy; `git bisect` will step into commits *inside* feature branches that were never expected to build on their own; and reverting requires `-m 1` with the re-merge trap attached (see the next section). This works well when feature branches are themselves disciplined — every commit builds and passes tests.

**Rebase and fast-forward.** The feature branch is rebased onto main and fast-forwarded in, producing a strictly linear history with no merge commits. Pros: `git log` is a straight line; every commit on main has exactly one parent, so bisect, blame, and `git log <file>` are maximally simple; each commit is a first-class reviewable unit. Cons: it demands discipline (the author must curate the branch into clean, individually-buildable commits before landing) and the true chronology is lost — commits appear in main in an order they never actually existed in.

**Squash and merge.** The whole PR collapses into one commit on main. Pros: main becomes a sequence of self-contained, atomic, revertable units; bisect granularity matches PR granularity, which is usually the right granularity; nobody has to curate intermediate commits, so authors can commit "wip" freely on their branch. Cons: intra-PR granularity is gone, so `git blame` on a 900-line squash tells you only "PR #4213", and a large PR becomes an indivisible bisect step. It also breaks reachability-based merge detection (`git branch --merged` misses squash-merged branches) and makes reusing the same branch after merging dangerous, because its old commits are still there and will come back on the next PR.

The way to choose is to ask what property you want main to have. In my experience the property worth optimising for is: **every commit on main is an independently buildable, independently revertable change.** Squash gets you that almost for free and is why it is the most common default for application repositories with PR-sized changes. Rebase-and-FF gets you that plus finer granularity, at the cost of requiring authors who know how to use `git rebase -i`; it suits repositories where individual commits are meaningfully atomic (kernels, libraries, infrastructure-as-code). Merge commits get you fidelity to what actually happened, which matters most when branch history is itself an audit artefact.

Whatever you pick, **enforce it in the platform**, not in a wiki page. Disable the merge methods you do not want in the repository settings, turn on "require linear history" if you chose rebase or squash, and require branches to be up to date (or better, use a merge queue) before merging. A repository where three merge strategies are all enabled produces a history that supports none of the workflows well.

Two operational notes that come up in follow-ups. First, squash-merge and long-lived shared branches interact badly: never squash-merge a branch that other branches are stacked on, because their base commits vanish and every stacked branch must be rebased with `--onto`. Second, if you use `pull.rebase`, be aware that a plain `git pull --rebase` on a branch that has upstream rewrites can silently replay your commits onto rewritten history; `git pull --rebase` is safe for your own topic branch and is *not* a substitute for coordinating a force-push on a shared one.

# Team-wide config that makes the policy the path of least resistance -----
git config --global pull.ff only            # never auto-merge on pull
git config --global pull.rebase true        # ... or explicitly rebase
git config --global rebase.autoStash true
git config --global rerere.enabled true
git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3
git config --global fetch.prune true
git config --global branch.sort -committerdate

# What the three policies look like on main -------------------------------
#
#  merge commits (--no-ff):        rebase + ff:            squash:
#    *   Merge PR #12               * feat: c3              * feat: whole PR #12
#    |\                             * feat: c2              * feat: whole PR #11
#    | * c3                         * feat: c1              * fix:  whole PR #10
#    | * c2                         * fix:  b1
#    | * c1                         * ...
#    |/
#    *   Merge PR #11

# Reading a merge-based history like a linear one -------------------------

# GitHub/GitLab settings that actually enforce the choice:
#   - allow ONLY the merge method you chose

#   - Require branches to be up to date (or use a merge queue)
#   - Automatically delete head branches after merge (critical for squash)

sections.title: 8. Interactive Rebase: History Surgery You Should Be Able to Do Cold
sections.content:
`git rebase -i <base>` opens an editor containing a *todo list* — one line per commit in the range, oldest first — and Git then executes that script. Editing the script is how you reorder, drop, combine, split, reword, and test commits. Interviewers ask about it because a candidate who can do this fluently can turn a messy exploratory branch into a reviewable one, which is a real force multiplier in code review.

The instructions you will actually use:

- `pick` — keep the commit as-is (the default for every line).
- `reword` — keep the changes, open an editor for a new message.
- `edit` — stop after applying this commit so you can amend it, split it, or run something.
- `squash` — combine into the previous commit and open an editor to combine both messages.
- `fixup` — combine into the previous commit and *discard* this commit's message.
- `drop` — delete the commit entirely (deleting the line does the same thing).
- `exec <cmd>` — run a shell command at this point; if it exits non-zero the rebase stops.
- `break` — stop here unconditionally, hand me a shell, continue when I say so.
- `label` / `reset` / `merge` — the topology instructions used by `--rebase-merges`.

Reordering is done by moving lines. Dropping is done by deleting lines. Git will warn you (via `rebase.missingCommitsCheck`) if you removed lines it thinks you did not mean to remove.

The workflow that makes this a daily tool rather than a stunt is **`--autosquash`**. While working, when you notice a mistake in an earlier commit, you do not amend it in place; you write a normal commit marked as belonging to that earlier one: `git commit --fixup=<sha>` (message becomes `fixup! <original subject>`) or `--squash=<sha>`. Later, `git rebase -i --autosquash <base>` automatically reorders those commits to sit directly after their targets and pre-sets their action to `fixup`/`squash`, so you usually just save and quit. Set `rebase.autoSquash = true` and this becomes the default for interactive rebases. This is how review feedback gets folded into the right commit instead of accumulating as a trail of "address review comments" commits.

**Splitting a commit** is the operation people cannot do under pressure, so learn it as a fixed recipe: mark the commit `edit`; when the rebase stops, run `git reset HEAD^` to un-commit it while keeping the changes in the working tree; then stage and commit in pieces (`git add -p` is your friend); then `git rebase --continue`.

**Verifying every commit** is what turns a curated branch from cosmetics into engineering. `git rebase -i --exec 'make test' origin/main` inserts an `exec make test` line after *every* commit in the range, so the rebase halts at the first commit that does not pass. If your policy is "every commit on main builds", this is how you actually check it rather than hoping. It is slow, so people run it before pushing a stack rather than on every rebase.

`git commit --amend` is the one-commit special case of all this: it creates a *new* commit replacing the current one (new hash, original author date preserved by default), and `--no-edit` keeps the message. `--amend` after pushing means a force-push, with all the caution that implies.

Two hazards to name in an interview. First, interactive rebase on commits others have pulled is the golden-rule violation, and `--autosquash` makes it easy to do accidentally on a shared branch. Second, a long interactive rebase that goes wrong is fully recoverable — `git rebase --abort` restores the exact pre-rebase state, and if you already finished, `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` or the reflog gets you back — so the correct response to a rebase gone sideways is to abort and retry with a smaller range, not to hand-fix the wreckage.

# A todo list, annotated ---------------------------------------------------
#   pick   a1b2c3d  feat: add token bucket
#   fixup  d4e5f6a  fixup! feat: add token bucket      <- folded in, msg dropped
#   reword b7c8d9e  add tests                          <- rename the commit
#   edit   c1d2e3f  refactor config loader             <- stop here to split it
#   drop   f4a5b6c  debug printf                       <- delete this commit
#   exec   make test                                   <- gate: stop if it fails
#   pick   9a8b7c6  docs: rate limiting

# The fixup workflow (this is the daily driver) ---------------------------
git commit --fixup=a1b2c3d                 # message: "fixup! feat: add token bucket"
git commit --squash=a1b2c3d                # same, but keeps the message for editing
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main     # auto-reorders and pre-marks them
git config --global rebase.autoSquash true

# Split one commit into three ---------------------------------------------
git rebase -i HEAD~4          # mark the target commit as: edit
# rebase stops on that commit:
git reset HEAD^               # un-commit, keep changes in the working tree
git add -p src/config.go      # stage the first logical piece interactively
git commit -m "config: extract loader"
git add -p src/config.go
git commit -m "config: add env override"
git add -A && git commit -m "config: docs"
git rebase --continue

# Prove every commit on the branch builds ---------------------------------
git rebase -i --exec 'make build && make test' origin/main
# equivalently, non-interactive:
git rebase --exec 'make test' origin/main

# Amend the last commit ----------------------------------------------------
git commit --amend --no-edit          # fold staged changes in, keep the message
git commit --amend --author="Priya <priya@example.com>"
git commit --amend --date=now

# Rewrite an old commit's author across a whole branch (rare, be careful)
git rebase -i --root --exec 'git commit --amend --no-edit --reset-author'

# Escape hatches -----------------------------------------------------------
git rebase --abort            # exact pre-rebase state
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD    # after a completed rebase you regret
git reflog                    # anything else

sections.title: 9. Cherry-pick, Revert, and the Merge-Revert Trap
sections.content:
`git cherry-pick <commit>` takes the *change* introduced by one commit and applies it to your current branch as a new commit. Mechanically it is a three-way merge where the base is the picked commit's parent, one side is the picked commit, and the other side is your HEAD. It therefore can conflict for exactly the reasons any merge can, and it produces a new commit ID, a new committer date, and — importantly — the original author preserved.

The main production use is **backporting a hotfix**. You fix a bug on trunk, then pick the fix onto the release branch that is currently in production. Always run it with `-x`, which appends a `(cherry picked from commit <sha>)` line to the message. That line is the only durable link between the two copies, and six months later during an incident it is what tells you the release branch's fix and trunk's fix are the same change.

The directionality matters more than the flags. **Fix on trunk first, then pick backwards to release branches.** If you fix directly on the release branch and rely on merging that branch forward later, any missed merge silently reintroduces the bug in the next release — a regression class that is genuinely common and genuinely embarrassing. Trunk-first guarantees the fix cannot be lost.

Cherry-picking creates duplicate content in two lineages, and Git handles that unevenly. `git rebase` deduplicates by patch-id and will silently drop your commit if an equivalent patch already exists upstream. `git merge` does *not* deduplicate; it three-way merges, and if both copies are byte-identical relative to the base the merge is clean, but if either side was subsequently touched you get a conflict that looks bizarre ("why is it conflicting, both sides have the same fix?"). `git cherry <upstream> <topic>` compares by patch-id and marks commits already present upstream with `-`, which is the tool for auditing "did every fix on the release branch make it back to trunk?"

`git revert <commit>` is the opposite discipline: instead of removing a commit from history, it computes the inverse patch and commits it forward. Nothing is rewritten, so it is safe on public branches, and the record shows both that the change happened and that it was undone. This is what you use in production. `git reset` is for private history; `git revert` is for anything anyone else has.

Now the trap, which is one of the highest-signal Git questions there is. **Reverting a merge commit.** A merge has two parents, so "the inverse patch" is ambiguous — Git needs to know which parent is the mainline you want to keep: `git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>` keeps the first parent (main) and undoes everything the side branch brought in. That works, and the code is correctly removed. But the merge commit itself is *still in the history and still reachable*. From Git's point of view the feature branch is merged. So when the team fixes the feature and tries to merge the branch again, Git computes a merge base that already includes those commits, concludes there is nothing new to bring in, and merges essentially nothing — the code does not come back. The bug reports read "I merged my branch and my code is missing."

There are two correct resolutions, and knowing both is the strong answer. Either **revert the revert** (`git revert <sha-of-the-revert-commit>`) before merging again, which restores the original content and lets subsequent commits on the branch merge normally; or **do not merge the old branch again** — create a fresh branch off current main and re-apply the work there, which is cleaner when the feature needs rework anyway. The general lesson to state out loud: reverting a merge undoes the *content* but not the *topology*, and Git's merge logic reasons about topology.

Prevention is better. If a feature might need to be pulled out, prefer squash-merging it (one commit, one clean revert, no `-m` ambiguity) or ship it behind a feature flag so "revert" means flipping a config value and takes thirty seconds instead of a merge argument.
sections.code:
# Backport a fix to a release branch --------------------------------------
git switch release/2.4
git cherry-pick -x 9f3c1ab            # -x records "(cherry picked from commit ...)"
# a range (exclusive of the first): everything after A up to and including B
git cherry-pick -x A..B
# pick a merge commit: say which parent's side to take
git cherry-pick -m 1 <merge-sha>
# stage without committing, e.g. to combine several picks
git cherry-pick -n 9f3c1ab 4b7de02 && git commit -m "backport: auth fixes"
# conflicts:
git cherry-pick --continue | --skip | --abort

# Audit: which fixes on release/2.4 are NOT on main? ----------------------
git cherry -v main release/2.4        # lines starting with '+' are missing upstream
#   - 9f3c1ab  already in main (same patch-id)
#   + 1122334  NOT in main            <-- investigate

# Revert on a public branch ------------------------------------------------
git revert 9f3c1ab                    # creates an inverse commit
git revert --no-commit A..B           # revert a range as one commit
git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>           # revert a MERGE, keeping first parent (main)

# ---- THE TRAP -----------------------------------------------------------
#  main:  ...--M1--R--------------X   (M1 = merge of feat, R = revert of M1)
#              /                 /
#  feat: ..--C1--C2----------C3-'     (re-merge X brings in ONLY C3)
#
#  After R, the code from C1/C2 is gone from main, but M1 still says
#  "feat is merged". Re-merging feat contributes nothing for C1/C2.
#
#  Fix A - restore, then merge normally:
git revert <sha-of-R>                 # revert the revert: C1/C2 content returns
git merge feat                        # now C3 merges on top as expected
#
#  Fix B - abandon the branch, redo the work on a fresh branch off main.
#
#  Prevention: squash-merge features (revert is then a single ordinary commit),
#  or ship behind a feature flag so "revert" is a config change.

sections.title: 10. Conflicts: What They Actually Are and How to Resolve Them Correctly
sections.content:
A conflict is not Git being confused. It is Git correctly reporting that it does not have enough information to decide. During a three-way merge, Git walks each file hunk by hunk and compares base, ours, and theirs. If only one side differs from the base, that side wins — no conflict. If both sides made the *same* change, they agree — no conflict. A conflict is exactly the case where both sides changed the same region relative to the base, and changed it differently.

There are also whole-file conflicts, which people forget until they hit one and Git says something they have never seen. **Modify/delete**: one side edited the file, the other deleted it — Git cannot know whether the edit should survive the deletion. **Add/add**: both sides created the same path with different content. **Rename/rename**: both sides moved the file, to different names. **Rename/modify**: one side moved it, the other edited it (Git usually resolves this by applying the edit at the new path, but it can conflict). **Directory/file**: one side has `logs` as a file, the other as a directory. Each of these prints a distinct message; read it rather than skimming to the conflict markers.

Underneath, a conflict lives in the **index as three stages** for the path: stage 1 base, stage 2 ours, stage 3 theirs. The working-tree file is a rendering of those with markers. `git add <file>` collapses the three stages into one and is what marks the path resolved — which is why "I fixed the file but Git still says conflicted" is always "you did not `git add` it".

**Turn on a better conflict style immediately.** The default `merge` style shows only ours and theirs, which forces you to guess what the original said. `merge.conflictStyle = diff3` adds the base between `|||||||` and `=======`, so you can see what each side *changed* rather than only what each side *has* — usually the difference between resolving in ten seconds and resolving wrongly. `zdiff3` (Git 2.35+) is diff3 with common leading/trailing lines hoisted out of the conflict region, giving you the same information in a tighter block. Set `zdiff3` and never look back.

**Turn on rerere.** `rerere.enabled = true` makes Git record the resolution of each conflicted hunk keyed by the conflict's content, and replay it automatically the next time the identical conflict appears. This is transformative in two situations: a long rebase where the same conflict recurs at every commit, and a long-lived branch that you repeatedly merge main into. Add `rerere.autoUpdate = true` and Git will stage the auto-resolved files for you. The caveat: rerere replays *your previous decision* silently, so if your first resolution was wrong, it will be wrong forever until you `git rerere forget <path>`.

**"Ours" and "theirs" invert during a rebase**, and this catches nearly everyone. In a merge, ours = the branch you are on, theirs = the branch being merged in. In a rebase, Git checks out the *new base* and replays your commits onto it, so from Git's perspective ours = the upstream you are rebasing onto, and theirs = the commit of yours being replayed. If you blindly `git checkout --ours` during a rebase you will throw away your own work. When in doubt, do not use ours/theirs shortcuts — read the diff.

Some files should never be textually merged, and `.gitattributes` is where you say so. Mark generated files and lockfiles with `merge=binary` or `-merge` so Git always produces a conflict instead of interleaving two machine-generated files into something that parses but is wrong; then resolve by regenerating (`npm install`, `go mod tidy`, `terraform providers lock`). Use `merge=union` for append-only files like a changelog, where taking both sides is always right. And set `* text=auto eol=lf` to kill the entire class of phantom conflicts caused by CRLF/LF churn between Windows and Linux checkouts.

Finally, the discipline: **resolve semantically, not textually**. The markers show you two texts, but the correct output is often neither side verbatim — it is the code that satisfies both intents. After every non-trivial resolution, build and run the tests before committing the merge. `git diff` (with no arguments, during a merge) shows a combined diff of your resolution against both parents, and `git log --merge -p <file>` shows only the commits from both sides that touched the conflicted file, which is the fastest way to recover the intent behind each change.
sections.code:
# Configure once ----------------------------------------------------------
git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3   # or diff3
git config --global rerere.enabled true
git config --global rerere.autoUpdate true

# What a zdiff3/diff3 conflict looks like ---------------------------------
#   <<<<<<< HEAD                (ours)
#   timeout = 30 * time.Second
#   ||||||| merged common ancestor
#   timeout = 10 * time.Second
#   =======
#   timeout = 60 * time.Second  (theirs)
#   >>>>>>> feat/slow-backend
#   -> base was 10. Ours tripled it, theirs sextupled it. Now you can
#      actually decide, instead of guessing which one was "the change".

# Triage a conflicted merge ------------------------------------------------
git status --short                # UU = both modified, DU/UD = delete conflicts
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U
git ls-files -u                   # the three index stages
git log --merge -p src/config.go  # only commits from both sides touching this file
git diff                          # during a merge: combined diff of your resolution

# Take one whole side of a file (know which side you mean!) ---------------
git checkout --ours   src/config.go     # merge: current branch | REBASE: upstream
git checkout --theirs src/config.go     # merge: incoming       | REBASE: your commit
git restore --source=MERGE_HEAD --worktree src/config.go
git checkout --conflict=diff3 src/config.go   # redraw the markers with the base

# Mark resolved and finish -------------------------------------------------
git add src/config.go
git merge --continue        # or: git rebase --continue / git cherry-pick --continue
git merge --abort           # give up cleanly

# Fix a wrong resolution rerere keeps replaying ----------------------------
git rerere status
git rerere diff
git rerere forget src/config.go

# .gitattributes: stop merging things that must not be merged -------------
#   package-lock.json   -merge            # always conflict; regenerate instead
#   go.sum              -merge
#   *.pbxproj           -merge
#   CHANGELOG.md        merge=union       # keep both sides' new lines
#   *.png               binary
#   * text=auto eol=lf                    # kill CRLF phantom conflicts

sections.title: 11. Reflog, Recovery, and Garbage Collection
sections.content:
The single most useful thing you can tell a panicking colleague is that Git almost never deletes anything immediately. Commits become *unreferenced*, not destroyed, and the reflog is the safety net that keeps them findable.

A reflog is a per-ref append-only log of every value that ref has held locally. `.git/logs/HEAD` records every move of HEAD; `.git/logs/refs/heads/main` records every move of `main`. Each line has the old ID, the new ID, who did it, when, and the command that caused it. Crucially the reflog is **local and per-clone** — it is not pushed, not fetched, and not present in a fresh clone. Your reflog and your colleague's reflog are different data, which is both a limitation (a fresh clone cannot recover your lost commit) and an opportunity (during an incident, the one machine that has not re-cloned holds the evidence).

Reflog syntax is deliberately distinct from ancestry syntax and mixing them up is a classic error. `HEAD~2` means two commits back in the graph. `HEAD@{2}` means the value HEAD had two moves ago in time, which may be on a completely different branch. Time expressions work too: `main@{yesterday}`, `HEAD@{2.hours.ago}`, `main@{2026-08-10}`.

The recovery recipes worth having memorised:

- **Bad `git reset --hard`**: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`. Also, reset/merge/rebase/pull all write `ORIG_HEAD` first, so `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` is the one-step undo for the most recent of those.
- **Deleted a branch**: `git reflog` (or the branch's own reflog if it still exists), find the tip, then `git branch <name> <sha>`. If the reflog is gone, `git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs` lists orphaned commits.
- **Rebase went wrong after it completed**: `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`, or find the pre-rebase tip in the reflog.
- **Amended away a good commit**: it is still in the reflog as the value before the amend.
- **Dropped or cleared a stash**: stash entries are commits, so `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit` and inspect candidates with `git show`, then `git stash apply <sha>`.
- **Staged but never committed, then reset --hard**: `git add` wrote the blob to the object database, so the *content* survives even though no commit references it. `git fsck --lost-found` writes dangling blobs into `.git/lost-found/other/`, named by hash; `grep` through them to find yours.

And the things the reflog cannot save, which you should say unprompted because it shows calibration: **anything never added to Git**. Uncommitted, unstaged working-tree edits destroyed by `git reset --hard` or `git checkout -- <file>` are gone. `git clean -fdx` deletes untracked files that were never in the object database — gone. Files excluded by `.gitignore` — gone. And anything at all once garbage collection has actually run after the reflog expired.

Which brings us to **gc**. Reachability is the rule: an object survives if it is reachable from a ref, the index, or an unexpired reflog entry. `gc.reflogExpire` defaults to 90 days for entries reachable from the ref's current tip, and `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable` defaults to 30 days for entries that are not. Unreachable loose objects are pruned only when older than `gc.pruneExpire`, which defaults to two weeks — that grace period exists so a concurrently-running Git command cannot have its half-built objects deleted underneath it. `git gc --auto` runs opportunistically when loose objects exceed `gc.auto` (default 6700) or packs exceed `gc.autoPackLimit`; `git maintenance` (Git 2.29+) is the modern, schedulable replacement that also keeps the commit-graph and multi-pack-index fresh.

Two operational corollaries. First, "I deleted the branch, so the secret is gone" is false: the blob remains reachable through the reflog for a month and through unreachable-object grace for two weeks, and on a hosting platform it may remain fetchable by SHA essentially indefinitely. Second, if you genuinely need to destroy local objects — after a history rewrite, for example — you must expire the reflog *and* prune explicitly, and even then every other clone and every fork still has them.
