# Look at what happened ---------------------------------------------------
git reflog                            # HEAD's movement log
git reflog show main                  # one branch's log
git reflog --date=iso HEAD | head -20
git log -g --oneline                  # reflog as a log (shows commit subjects)

#   a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
#   9f8e7d6 HEAD@{1}: commit: add retry budget      <-- the thing you want back
#   4c3b2a1 HEAD@{2}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feat

# ---- Recovery cookbook --------------------------------------------------
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}             # undo a bad reset
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD            # undo the last merge/rebase/reset/pull

git branch rescue 9f8e7d6             # resurrect a deleted branch tip
git switch -c rescue 9f8e7d6

# reflog gone / fresh clone: search the object database directly
git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs
git fsck --lost-found                 # writes dangling objects to .git/lost-found/
git show <dangling-sha>               # identify candidates
grep -rl "the string I lost" .git/lost-found/other/

# Recover a dropped stash --------------------------------------------------
git fsck --unreachable | awk '/commit/ {print $3}' \
  | xargs -I{} git log -1 --format='%h %ci %s' {} | grep -i 'WIP on'
git stash apply <sha>

# Someone force-pushed over main -------------------------------------------
#  1. DO NOT let anyone re-clone or gc yet.
#  2. On any machine that still has the old main:
git reflog show origin/main           # remote-tracking refs have reflogs too
git push --force-with-lease origin <good-sha>:main
#  3. If no local copy survives, ask the host: GitHub's events API and
#     GitLab's activity/reflog features can still surface the old SHA, and
#     the objects usually remain fetchable by SHA until the server gc's.

# ---- Garbage collection ---------------------------------------------------
git count-objects -vH
git gc                                # normal, respects the grace periods
git maintenance start                 # scheduled background upkeep (2.29+)

# Actually destroy unreachable local objects (irreversible) ---------------
git reflog expire --expire=now --expire-unreachable=now --all
git gc --prune=now --aggressive

# Defaults worth knowing:
#   gc.reflogExpire             90 days   (reachable reflog entries)
#   gc.reflogExpireUnreachable  30 days
#   gc.pruneExpire              2 weeks   (unreachable loose objects)
#   gc.auto                     6700 loose objects triggers auto gc

sections.title: 12. git bisect: Binary Search Over History
sections.content:
`git bisect` finds the commit that introduced a change in behaviour by binary search. You tell it one commit where the behaviour is bad and one where it is good; it checks out something roughly halfway between (in the DAG, not in date order), you test, you tell it good or bad, and it halves the candidate set again. Over 1,000 commits that is about ten tests instead of a thousand. Interviewers like bisect because it separates people who debug by reading code from people who debug by narrowing the search space, and because the interesting content is entirely in the failure modes.

The manual loop is `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad`, `git bisect good <old-rev>`, then repeated `git bisect good` / `git bisect bad`, and finally `git bisect reset` to return to where you started. Git puts you in detached HEAD at each step; nothing about your branches changes.

The version you should actually reach for is **`git bisect run <script>`**, which automates the whole thing. The contract is exit-code based and precise, so state it correctly: **exit 0 means good/old; exit 1–127 except 125 means bad/new; exit 125 means "cannot test this commit", which is equivalent to `git bisect skip`; and any other exit code (128–255) aborts the bisect entirely.** The 125 case is the one that matters in practice — it is how you tell Git "this commit does not build, do not count it as bad", and forgetting it is the number one reason automated bisects produce wrong answers.

Bisect also generalises past "find the bug". The good/bad vocabulary is just labels, and `git bisect terms --term-old=<x> --term-new=<y>` renames them, so you can bisect for *when something was fixed*, when a performance number crossed a threshold, or when a binary's size grew. That reframing — bisect finds the commit where any boolean predicate over the tree flips — is the answer that shows you understand the tool rather than the recipe.

Now the failure modes, which is where the interview actually lives.

**Flaky tests destroy bisect.** Binary search assumes a deterministic oracle. A test that fails 30% of the time will hand Git a wrong answer and the search will confidently converge on an innocent commit. The fixes: make the reproducer deterministic first, or run it N times in the script and only report good if all N pass (biasing toward "bad" is usually safer, since a false "good" prunes the half containing the real culprit).

**Commits that do not build.** In a merge-based history, many commits are mid-feature states from inside branches that were never expected to compile. Return 125 for those. `git bisect --first-parent` (available in recent Git) restricts the search to the mainline, which sidesteps the problem entirely on a merge-based main and correctly identifies the *merge* as the introduction point — often exactly what you want, since the merge is the unit that shipped.

**Environment drift.** Bisecting six months back means checking out code whose dependencies, toolchain, or database schema no longer match your machine. The script, not your shell, must own the environment: install dependencies inside the script, or build and test inside a container whose base image is pinned per-commit. Also make sure the script does not accidentally test stale build artefacts — clean between steps or you will bisect your build cache.

**The script lives outside the repo.** Bisect checks out old trees; if your test script is in the repository it will be replaced (or deleted) at each step. Keep it in `/tmp` and pass an absolute path.

**Dirty working tree.** Bisect refuses to run with uncommitted changes it would clobber; commit or stash first. And if you need a temporary patch applied at every step (a debug print, a workaround for an unrelated breakage), apply it inside the script and revert it before exiting.

Finally, `git bisect log` and `git bisect replay` let you record a session, correct a mistaken good/bad answer, and re-run it — which you will want the first time you realise you mislabelled step three.
sections.code:
# Manual bisect -----------------------------------------------------------
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current HEAD is broken
git bisect good v2.3.0         # this tag was fine
# ... git checks out a midpoint; test it, then:
git bisect good      |  git bisect bad      |  git bisect skip
git bisect log                 # transcript (save it!)
git bisect reset               # return to the original HEAD

# Automated: the exit-code contract ---------------------------------------
#   0        -> good / old
#   1..127   -> bad / new        (except 125)
#   125      -> untestable, skip this commit
#   128..255 -> abort the bisect
git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0 --      # bad first, then good, in one line
git bisect run /tmp/check.sh         # ABSOLUTE path: the repo tree changes under you

# /tmp/check.sh -----------------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
# 1. Build. If it cannot build, this commit is untestable, NOT bad.
if ! make -s build >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  exit 125
fi
# 2. Defeat flakiness: 5 clean runs required to call it good.
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  if ! ./bin/app --selftest >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    exit 1                            # bad
  fi
done
exit 0                                # good

# Bisect on a threshold, not a crash --------------------------------------
#   exit 1 if p99 latency regressed past 250ms
test "$(./bench --json | jq '.p99_ms')" -lt 250

# Bisect for a FIX instead of a bug ---------------------------------------
git bisect start
git bisect terms --term-old=broken --term-new=fixed
git bisect fixed            # HEAD works now
git bisect broken v2.3.0    # it was broken here

# Only consider the mainline (merge-based history) ------------------------
git bisect start --first-parent
# -> blames the MERGE that introduced the regression, and never checks out
#    half-finished commits from inside feature branches.

# Limit to a subdirectory (fewer candidate commits) -----------------------
git bisect start -- services/auth/

# Fix a mislabelled step --------------------------------------------------
git bisect log > /tmp/bisect.log     # edit the wrong line out
git bisect reset
git bisect replay /tmp/bisect.log

sections.title: 13. Stash and Worktrees: Parking Work Without Losing It
sections.content:
`git stash` looks like a magic scratch buffer, but it is built out of ordinary commits, and knowing that is what lets you recover from its failure modes. When you run `git stash push`, Git creates a commit representing your current index, then a commit representing your working tree whose first parent is HEAD and whose second parent is that index commit, and if you passed `-u` a third parent holding your untracked files. It then points `refs/stash` at the working-tree commit and resets your working tree and index back to HEAD. You can verify all of this with `git cat-file -p refs/stash` and count the parents.

The "stack" is not a stack data structure — it is `refs/stash` plus that ref's reflog. `stash@{2}` is reflog syntax meaning "the value refs/stash held two moves ago". This explains several behaviours: `git stash list` is really a reflog listing, dropping an entry rewrites the reflog rather than deleting an object, and dropped stashes remain recoverable via `git fsck` until garbage collection.

The pitfalls, in order of how often they bite people:

**Untracked files are not stashed by default.** `git stash` only touches tracked files. The classic disaster is stash-then-`git clean -fd` to get a pristine tree: the clean deletes exactly the untracked files the stash did not save, and since they were never in the object database, nothing can bring them back. Use `-u` (untracked) or `-a` (untracked plus ignored — careful, that includes `node_modules` and `.env`).

**`pop` is `apply` plus `drop`, and it only drops on success.** If applying conflicts, the entry stays in the list. Good — but people then resolve the conflict, forget the entry is still there, and pop it a second time later. Prefer `apply` plus an explicit `drop` when you care.

**The index is not restored by default.** `git stash pop` puts everything back as unstaged working-tree changes, flattening your carefully staged/unstaged split. `--index` restores it.

**A stash is not a branch and not a backup.** It is local-only, invisible to `git status`, unnamed unless you pass `-m`, and easy to accumulate — every team has someone with 40 stash entries from 2023 that nobody dares delete. Anything you will not resume within an hour or two belongs in a WIP commit on a branch, which is visible, pushable, and named.

**Stash does not handle submodule state**, and applying a stash across branches with very different content is just a merge and can conflict.

The better tool for the most common reason people stash — "I need to look at something else right now" — is **`git worktree`**. `git worktree add ../hotfix -b hotfix origin/main` creates a second working directory with its own HEAD, its own index, and its own checked-out branch, backed by the *same* object database. Nothing is stashed, nothing is rebuilt, your original build artefacts and running dev server stay exactly as they were, and switching contexts is `cd`. Worktrees are how you review a colleague's PR while your own compile is running, how you keep a permanent tree pinned to `main` for comparison, and how CI agents check out multiple refs without re-cloning a large repository.

Worktrees have their own rules. Git will refuse to check out the same branch in two worktrees at once (that would let two indexes fight over one ref) — use `--detach` if you truly want the same commit twice. Deleting the directory by hand leaves stale administrative files in `.git/worktrees`, so use `git worktree remove` or run `git worktree prune`. And `git worktree lock` prevents pruning of a worktree on removable media. In a monorepo, worktrees plus a shared object store are a large part of how people avoid five 20 GB clones on one laptop.
sections.code:
# Stash is made of commits - prove it ------------------------------------
git stash push -u -m "wip: retry backoff"
git cat-file -p refs/stash | head -5
#   tree   313ab5c...
#   parent afa4cdf...   <- HEAD when stashed
#   parent 7e59cd8...   <- the INDEX state
#   parent 883c9e0...   <- the UNTRACKED files (only with -u)
git reflog refs/stash              # this is what `git stash list` reads

# Everyday usage -----------------------------------------------------------
git stash push -m "msg" -- src/auth/    # only these paths
git stash push -u                        # INCLUDE untracked  <- usually what you want
git stash push -a                        # + ignored files (node_modules, .env: careful)
git stash push -S                        # only the STAGED changes (Git 2.35+)
git stash push -k                        # keep the index staged (test what you'll commit)
git stash push -p                        # choose hunks interactively

git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{1}              # full diff of an entry
git stash apply --index stash@{1}        # restore staged/unstaged split too
git stash pop                            # apply + drop (drops ONLY if apply succeeded)
git stash branch fix/from-stash stash@{0}  # new branch at the stash's base, then apply

# Recover a dropped stash --------------------------------------------------
git fsck --unreachable | awk '/commit/{print $3}' \
  | xargs -I{} git log -1 --format='%h %ci %s' {} | grep 'WIP on'
git stash apply <sha>

# The trap -----------------------------------------------------------------
git stash          # tracked files only
git clean -fd      # DELETES the untracked files the stash did not save. Unrecoverable.
#   -> always `git stash push -u` before cleaning, or `git clean -nd` (dry run) first.

# Worktrees: the better answer to "I need to switch context" -------------
git worktree add ../hotfix -b hotfix origin/main   # second dir, same object db
git worktree add ../review --detach origin/pr-1234
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../hotfix
git worktree prune                                  # clean up after rm -rf'd dirs
# Note: the same branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees at once.

sections.title: 14. Remotes, fetch vs pull, and Force-Push Safety
sections.content:
A remote is a name for a URL plus a **refspec** — a rule mapping refs on the other side to refs in your repository. The default fetch refspec, `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*`, says: take every branch on origin and store it locally under `refs/remotes/origin/`, and the leading `+` means allow non-fast-forward updates to those local copies. Those `refs/remotes/*` refs are **remote-tracking branches**: your cached snapshot of what the remote looked like at your last fetch. They are not live. `origin/main` is not "main on the server"; it is "main on the server as of the last time I fetched".

`git fetch` updates those tracking refs and downloads the objects they need, and does nothing else. It cannot break your working tree and cannot lose work. `git pull` is `fetch` followed by an integration step — merge by default, rebase if configured. The reason experienced people say "do not use bare `git pull`" is not that pull is broken; it is that the integration step happens before you have looked at what arrived, and with the default merge behaviour a divergent branch silently gains a `Merge branch 'main' of ...` commit. Since Git 2.27 Git warns when a pull would need to reconcile divergent branches and no strategy is configured, which is a nudge toward setting the policy explicitly. The safe configuration is `pull.ff = only`, so a pull either fast-forwards or stops and tells you, at which point you consciously choose `git rebase origin/main` or `git merge origin/main`.

Pushing is the mirror image. `git push` sends objects and asks the remote to update a ref, and the remote **refuses non-fast-forward updates** by default — that is the protection that stops you from erasing someone's commits. `--force` disables it entirely and is the wrong tool almost always.

**`--force-with-lease`** is the right tool, and you should be able to explain its mechanism, not just its name. It sends the value you *believe* the remote ref currently holds — taken from your remote-tracking ref — and the server rejects the push if the actual value differs. So if a colleague pushed after your last fetch, the lease is stale and the push is refused instead of destroying their commit.

Its hole is the good follow-up question. The lease is checked against your *remote-tracking ref*, and anything that fetches updates that ref: an explicit `git fetch`, an IDE that polls in the background, a shell prompt that fetches for its status indicator. Once the tracking ref has quietly advanced to include your colleague's commit, the lease matches reality, the push succeeds, and their work is gone — the safety was silently disarmed. **`--force-if-includes`** (Git 2.30+) closes this: used alongside `--force-with-lease`, it additionally requires that the remote's current tip is actually reachable from your local reflog — that is, that you genuinely saw and integrated the remote state, rather than merely having fetched it in the background. Configure `push.useForceIfIncludes = true` and stop thinking about it.

The operational rules around force-pushing: never to a shared branch; block it at the platform for `main` and release branches via branch protection; on your own PR branch it is normal and expected (that is what rebasing a PR means); and always tell reviewers, because a force-push invalidates in-flight review comments on the old commits.

Recovery when someone does force-push over a protected branch is a scenario question worth rehearsing. Step one is to stop the bleeding: freeze pushes and tell people not to re-clone, because a machine that still has the old objects is your best recovery source. Step two: `git reflog show origin/main` on any such machine — remote-tracking refs have reflogs too — gives the pre-force SHA, and `git push --force-with-lease origin <good-sha>:main` restores it. If no local copy survives, the host usually still has the objects: GitHub's events API records the old and new SHAs of pushes, and objects generally remain fetchable by SHA until the server garbage-collects. Step three is prevention: enable branch protection, and enable it on release branches too, not just `main`.

Two more things worth knowing. `git push --atomic` makes a multi-ref push all-or-nothing, which matters when you are pushing a commit and its tag together. And in CI, `--depth` shallow clones are fast but break `git describe`, `git merge-base`, and blame; `git fetch --unshallow` or `--filter=blob:none` (a partial clone, which keeps full history but fetches file contents lazily) is usually the better trade.
sections.code:
# Refspecs: what fetch actually does --------------------------------------
git config --get-all remote.origin.fetch
#   +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*
git fetch origin                       # update refs/remotes/origin/*, touch nothing else
git fetch --prune                      # delete tracking refs for branches deleted upstream
git fetch origin 'refs/pull/*/head:refs/remotes/origin/pr/*'   # fetch GitHub PR refs

# Make pull predictable ----------------------------------------------------
git config --global pull.ff only       # fast-forward or stop and tell me
# then integrate on purpose:
git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main     # linear
git fetch origin && git merge  origin/main     # merge commit
# or commit to rebasing always:
git config --global pull.rebase true

# Safe force-push ----------------------------------------------------------
git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes
git config --global push.useForceIfIncludes true
git config --global push.default simple

#  --force               : "overwrite whatever is there"          NEVER on shared refs
#  --force-with-lease    : "overwrite only if the remote is still at the value my
#                           remote-tracking ref says"  -- defeated by a background fetch
#  --force-if-includes   : "...and only if I have actually integrated that value,
#                           proven by my reflog"        (Git 2.30+)

# Pushing to a different name / deleting refs ------------------------------
git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/release/2.5
git push origin --delete old-branch
git push origin :old-branch            # same thing, older spelling
git push --atomic origin main v2.5.0   # both refs update, or neither

# Someone force-pushed over main - recovery --------------------------------
# 1. Freeze pushes. Tell everyone NOT to re-clone or run gc.
# 2. On a machine that fetched before the force-push:
git reflog show origin/main
#   7ab19c2 refs/remotes/origin/main@{1}: fetch: fast-forward   <- the good tip
git push --force-with-lease origin 7ab19c2:main
# 3. No local copy? The objects usually still exist server-side:
#    - GitHub: the events API records before/after SHAs of every push;
#      `git fetch origin <sha>` often still works until the server gc's.
# 4. Turn on branch protection for main AND release/* so it cannot recur.

# CI clone strategies -------------------------------------------------------
git clone --depth=1 <url>                    # fastest; breaks describe/merge-base/blame
git fetch --unshallow                        # repair a shallow clone
git clone --filter=blob:none <url>           # full history, file contents on demand
git clone --filter=tree:0 --sparse <url>     # most aggressive; for huge monorepos

sections.title: 15. Hooks: Local Convenience, Server-Side Enforcement
sections.content:
A hook is an executable file in `.git/hooks/` that Git runs at a defined point in an operation. If the hook exits non-zero, the operation aborts (for the hooks that are defined as gates). There is nothing more to the mechanism — no plugin API, no manifest, just a program with the right name and the executable bit set. Git ships `.sample` versions of each so you can see the names.

The client-side hooks you will actually use: **pre-commit** runs before the commit message is requested and is where linters and formatters go; **prepare-commit-msg** can pre-populate the message (injecting a ticket ID parsed from the branch name is the classic); **commit-msg** validates the finished message and is where Conventional Commits or DCO sign-off checks live; **pre-push** runs before objects are sent and is the right place for anything slow enough that you do not want it on every commit, such as the full unit-test suite or a "refuse to push directly to main" guard; **post-checkout** and **post-merge** are useful for re-running dependency installation when a lockfile changed; and **pre-rebase** can protect specific branches from being rebased.

Three facts about client hooks that must be in your answer. First, **hooks are not versioned and not cloned**. `.git/` is not part of the tree, so a hook you write does not reach your teammates. The clean fix is `core.hooksPath` (Git 2.9+), which points Git at a directory *inside* the repository — commit `.githooks/`, set `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` in your bootstrap script, and now hooks are code-reviewed like everything else. This is exactly what husky, lefthook, and the `pre-commit` framework automate; they also solve the "new joiner forgot to run the bootstrap" problem by installing on `npm install` or similar.

Second, **hooks are trivially bypassed**. `git commit --no-verify` skips pre-commit and commit-msg; `git push --no-verify` skips pre-push. Anyone can also just delete the file. Therefore: client hooks are a *fast feedback* mechanism, never a *control*. If a rule must hold — no secrets in commits, no direct pushes to main, DCO required, protected paths need approval — it has to be enforced somewhere the developer cannot skip.

Third, **slow hooks get disabled**. A pre-commit hook that takes fifteen seconds will train the whole team to type `--no-verify` reflexively, at which point you have negative value: the checks do not run *and* everyone has a habit of bypassing. Budget roughly a second or two for pre-commit. Achieve that by operating only on staged files rather than the whole tree, and push whole-repository checks to pre-push or CI.

Server-side hooks are the enforcement layer. **pre-receive** runs once with all ref updates on stdin and rejects the entire push if it exits non-zero — this is the all-or-nothing gate for secret scanning, protected-path rules, commit-message policy, and maximum object size. **update** runs once per ref, so it can reject some refs and accept others. **post-receive** runs after everything is accepted and is where you trigger CI, notify chat, or kick off a deployment. On hosted platforms you usually cannot install these — GitHub Enterprise Server and self-managed GitLab support server hooks, but github.com does not — so the equivalent controls are branch protection rules, required status checks, push rulesets, required reviews, CODEOWNERS, and secret-scanning push protection. Say this explicitly in an interview: *the SaaS-equivalent of pre-receive is branch protection plus required checks*.

The practical failure modes are unglamorous and common: the hook file is not executable (`chmod +x`), it has no shebang or a wrong one, it assumes a TTY and therefore breaks in GUI clients and IDEs that run Git with no terminal, it depends on tools that are on your `PATH` but not on a colleague's, or it makes a network call and hangs when the VPN is down. A subtler one: a pre-commit hook that auto-formats files writes to the *working tree*, but the commit is built from the *index* — so the reformatted version is not what gets committed unless the hook re-stages, and re-staging blindly can sweep in unrelated unstaged changes. The safe patterns are to format only the staged content, or to fail the commit and tell the user to run the formatter, rather than silently mutating their tree.
sections.code:
# Version your hooks -------------------------------------------------------
mkdir -p .githooks
git config core.hooksPath .githooks       # per-repo; put it in the bootstrap script
chmod +x .githooks/*                      # forgetting this is failure mode #1

# .githooks/pre-commit -----------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# Only look at STAGED files, and only ones that still exist (not deletions).
files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM -- '*.go')
[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0
if ! gofmt -l $files | grep -q .; then exit 0; fi
echo "These staged files are not gofmt'd:"; gofmt -l $files
echo "Run: gofmt -w $files"
exit 1        # fail loudly; do NOT silently rewrite the user's working tree

# .githooks/commit-msg -----------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
pattern='^(feat|fix|docs|refactor|test|chore|perf|build|ci)(\([a-z0-9-]+\))?!?: .{1,72}'
head -1 "$1" | grep -Eq "$pattern" || {
  echo "Commit message must follow Conventional Commits, e.g."
  echo "  fix(auth): stop retrying on 401"
  exit 1
}

# .githooks/pre-push -- refuse to push directly to protected branches -----
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
protected='^refs/heads/(main|master|release/.*)$'
while read -r _local_ref _local_sha remote_ref _remote_sha; do
  if [[ "$remote_ref" =~ $protected ]]; then
    echo "Direct push to $remote_ref is not allowed. Open a PR."
    exit 1
  fi
done

# Server side: pre-receive, the gate that cannot be skipped ---------------
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# stdin: <old-sha> <new-sha> <ref-name>, one line per ref being updated
set -euo pipefail
zero=0000000000000000000000000000000000000000
while read -r old new ref; do
  [ "$new" = "$zero" ] && continue                   # branch deletion: nothing to scan
  if [ "$old" = "$zero" ]; then
    # New branch: only the commits not already reachable from any existing ref,
    # otherwise you rescan the entire history on every branch creation.
    revs=$(git rev-list "$new" --not --all)
  else
    revs=$(git rev-list "$old..$new")
  fi
  for sha in $revs; do
    if git show --pretty=format: --name-only "$sha" | grep -qiE '\.pem$|id_rsa'; then
      echo "REJECTED $ref: commit $sha adds a private key"; exit 1
    fi
  done
  # Any blob over 50MB in the new tip's tree?  ls-tree -l column 4 is the size.
  if git ls-tree -r -l "$new" | awk '$4 > 52428800 {found=1} END {exit !found}'; then
    echo "REJECTED $ref: contains a file larger than 50MB - use Git LFS"; exit 1
  fi
done
# Exit non-zero and the WHOLE push is rejected atomically.

# Bypasses you must assume exist -------------------------------------------
git commit --no-verify        # skips pre-commit and commit-msg
git push   --no-verify        # skips pre-push
#  -> client hooks are feedback, not policy. Real policy lives in
#     pre-receive (self-hosted) or branch protection + required status
#     checks + CODEOWNERS + secret-scanning push protection (SaaS).

sections.title: 16. Submodules, Subtrees, and Vendoring
sections.content:
A submodule is a pointer from one repository into another, and the mechanism is smaller than people expect. In the superproject's tree there is an entry with mode **160000** — a *gitlink* — whose object ID is a commit SHA that does not exist in this repository at all. Alongside it, a tracked file `.gitmodules` maps each such path to a URL. That is the whole design: the superproject pins an exact commit of the child, and knows where to get it.

The consequences of that design are the interview content. Because the superproject stores only a commit ID, checking out the superproject does **not** populate the submodule — you get an empty directory until `git submodule update --init --recursive` runs, or you cloned with `--recurse-submodules`. Because the pin is a raw commit ID with no branch attached, a submodule checkout is in **detached HEAD** by default, which is why work done inside a submodule is so easy to lose: you edit, commit, switch something in the parent, and your commit is now unreferenced.

And because the child's objects live in a different repository, **push order matters absolutely**. If you commit in the submodule, then commit the updated gitlink in the superproject, then push only the superproject, everyone else — and CI — gets a gitlink pointing at a commit that does not exist on the remote. The error is `fatal: reference is not a tree: <sha>` or "Failed to clone ... Please make sure you have the correct access rights". This is the single most common submodule outage, and the fix is to always push the submodule first (or `git push --recurse-submodules=on-demand`, which does it for you).

More friction worth naming: merges and rebases can conflict on the gitlink itself, and the conflict is a pair of commit IDs with no textual content, so you must decide which child commit is correct and `git add` the path. Everyone who clones needs *read access to every submodule repository*, which turns a private dependency into an onboarding and CI-credentials problem. Branch switching in the parent does not switch the submodule unless `submodule.recurse` is set. And tooling — IDEs, `git grep`, CI checkout actions, blame across the boundary — all need extra configuration.

Given all that, submodules are the right answer in a narrow set of cases: you need to pin an exact upstream commit, the child genuinely is a separate repository with its own release cadence, and you want the parent to record which version it depends on in a way that is auditable in Git itself. Vendored forks of third-party code, shared proto/schema repositories, and infrastructure module libraries are the honest use cases.

**git subtree** is the alternative that trades pinning for simplicity. `git subtree add --prefix=vendor/lib <url> <ref> --squash` copies the other project's files *into* your tree as ordinary files and records the import in your history. There is no `.gitmodules`, no extra clone step, no detached HEAD, and nothing special for CI to do — a plain clone gets everything. The cost is that your repository now contains that code (so it grows), updating is an explicit `git subtree pull`, and contributing changes back upstream via `git subtree push` is workable but clunky. If most of your team consumes the dependency and rarely modifies it, subtree is usually the kinder choice.

The third option, and often the right one, is to **not use Git for dependencies at all**. If the child produces a versioned artefact — a Go module, an npm package, a container image, a Terraform module in a registry — then a package manager gives you semantic versioning, a lockfile, a checksum, transitive resolution, and a CDN, all of which submodules approximate poorly. The strongest interview answer to "submodules or subtrees?" is usually: "for third-party code, a package registry; for tightly-coupled internal code, a monorepo; and submodules only when I need a Git-native pin to an exact commit of a repo I do not control." Say what you would do first, then explain the mechanism if pushed.

# What a submodule really is ----------------------------------------------
git ls-tree HEAD vendor/libfoo
#   160000 commit 4a2f0b1c...    vendor/libfoo      <- gitlink: a commit id
cat .gitmodules
#   [submodule "vendor/libfoo"]
#       path = vendor/libfoo
#       url  = https://github.com/acme/libfoo.git
#       branch = main            # only used by `git submodule update --remote`

# Clone / init ------------------------------------------------------------
git clone --recurse-submodules <url>
git submodule update --init --recursive          # after a plain clone
git submodule update --init --recursive --depth 1   # CI: shallow children
git config --global submodule.recurse true       # switch/pull/checkout recurse too

# Update the pin to the child's latest upstream ---------------------------
git submodule update --remote vendor/libfoo      # moves to the branch tip
git add vendor/libfoo && git commit -m "bump libfoo to $(git -C vendor/libfoo rev-parse --short HEAD)"

# THE failure mode: push order --------------------------------------------
#   WRONG: commit in child -> commit gitlink in parent -> push parent only
#          => everyone else: "fatal: reference is not a tree: 4a2f0b1c"
#   RIGHT:
git -C vendor/libfoo push origin HEAD:main
git push origin main
#   or make Git do it:
git push --recurse-submodules=on-demand
git config push.recurseSubmodules check          # refuse to push if child is unpushed

# Work inside a submodule without losing commits --------------------------
git -C vendor/libfoo switch -c fix/parse-bug     # detached HEAD by default: attach one
git -C vendor/libfoo commit -am "fix parse bug"
git -C vendor/libfoo push -u origin fix/parse-bug

# Inspect / debug ----------------------------------------------------------
git submodule status --recursive        # '-' not initialised, '+' differs from pin
git submodule foreach 'git status -s'
git diff --submodule=log                # show child commits between two pins

# Conflicted gitlink during a merge ---------------------------------------
#   both sides changed vendor/libfoo to different commits
git -C vendor/libfoo log --oneline <ours-sha>..<theirs-sha>   # decide which is right
git -C vendor/libfoo checkout <chosen-sha>
git add vendor/libfoo

# Removing a submodule properly -------------------------------------------
git submodule deinit -f vendor/libfoo
git rm -f vendor/libfoo
rm -rf .git/modules/vendor/libfoo

# The alternative: subtree (content is copied INTO your repo) -------------
git subtree add  --prefix=vendor/libfoo https://github.com/acme/libfoo.git main --squash
git subtree pull --prefix=vendor/libfoo https://github.com/acme/libfoo.git main --squash
git subtree push --prefix=vendor/libfoo https://github.com/acme/libfoo.git contrib
#  + plain clone just works, no init step, no CI credentials for the child
#  - your repo grows; no exact-commit pin recorded as such; pushing back is clunky

sections.title: 17. Branching Models: Trunk-Based, GitFlow, and Why Lifetime Is the Variable
sections.content:
Branching models are process, but the reasoning behind them is technical: **the cost of integration grows superlinearly with how long you defer it**, so a branching model is really a policy about how long code is allowed to live unintegrated. Every model that works does so by keeping that interval short or by paying a heavy tax to manage it.

**GitFlow** (Vincent Driessen, 2010) defines five branch classes: `master` holds released code, `develop` is the integration branch, `feature/*` branch off and back into develop, `release/*` branches stabilise a release and merge into both master and develop, and `hotfix/*` branch off master and merge back into both. It is internally consistent and it solved a real problem: shipping versioned, installed software where several releases are supported simultaneously and a release must be stabilised for weeks while new development continues. Its costs are exactly what you would predict — two long-lived integration branches that constantly drift apart, features that sit unintegrated until a release window, and a merge graph that requires diagrams. Driessen himself later added a note to the original article saying it is not the right model for continuously-delivered web applications. Say that in an interview; it demonstrates you know the model rather than just disliking it.

**GitHub Flow** is the minimal version: `main` is always deployable, all work happens on short-lived branches, changes land through pull requests, and deployment happens from `main`. It is the default for most SaaS teams and works well up to a fairly large size.

**Trunk-based development** is the same idea taken seriously. Everyone integrates into trunk at least daily; branches, if used at all, live hours rather than days; incomplete work ships to production disabled behind **feature flags** rather than being held back on a branch; and release branches, if they exist, are cut from trunk purely for stabilisation with fixes cherry-picked from trunk rather than developed on the branch. This is the model behind the very high deployment frequencies reported by the DORA research, and the causal claim in that research is specific: trunk-based development and short-lived branches are among the practices that correlate with high software delivery performance.

The mechanism to articulate is why short branches win. Integration is where risk concentrates, because that is where independent assumptions collide. Deferring integration does not remove that risk; it batches it, and batched risk arrives at the worst moment, right before a release, all at once, with several authors who have paged out the context. Short-lived branches also make conflicts small and semantic conflicts rare, keep CI signal meaningful (a green build on a branch that is two hours behind trunk means something; two weeks behind it means very little), and make revert a viable rollback strategy because each landed change is small.

Feature flags are the enabling technology, and they are not free. A flag is a runtime branch, so the number of code paths grows combinatorially, tests must cover at least the flag states that will exist in production, and stale flags become a permanent tax. A real flag discipline has an owner and a removal date per flag, an audit of flags older than some threshold, and a rule that flags controlling incomplete features default to off and are removed once fully rolled out. Without that discipline, teams trade merge debt for flag debt.

Release management on trunk: cut `release/x.y` from trunk when you need to stabilise, fix bugs on trunk first and cherry-pick onto the release branch (never the reverse, or fixes get lost on the next release), tag the exact shipped commit, and delete or archive the branch once the release is retired. For libraries with multiple supported majors you will keep several such branches alive, and that is fine — the point is that no *feature development* happens on them.

The honest interview answer to "which model would you use?" is conditional: continuously-deployed service with one production version → trunk-based with flags; a mobile app or on-prem product with real release trains and multiple supported versions → trunk plus release branches, which is most of GitFlow's value without `develop`; a small team shipping a web app → GitHub Flow. And add the meta-point: whatever you choose, encode it in branch protection rules and CI configuration so the model is enforced by the tooling rather than by documentation nobody reads.

#               \             /          /
#   release      \        ●──●──────────/          stabilise only
#                 \      /             /
#   develop  ──●───●──●─●─────●───●───●            integration branch
#               \ /       \ /

# Trunk-based (continuous delivery) ---------------------------------------

# ... fix, PR, merge to main first ...

git cherry-pick -x <fix-sha>        # -x records the provenance

    return newPricing(ctx, order)
}

sections.title: 18. Pull Request Etiquette, Review, and Merge Queues
sections.content:
Code review is the highest-leverage quality control most teams have, and pull request hygiene is what determines whether it works. Interviewers ask about it because it is a direct proxy for whether you are pleasant and effective to work with at scale.

**Size dominates everything.** Review effectiveness falls off sharply as diffs grow; the widely-cited industry review data (the Cisco/SmartBear study is the usual reference) puts useful review throughput in the low hundreds of lines per hour and finds defect-detection dropping off well before a diff reaches four hundred lines. The behavioural effect is even stronger than the statistical one: a 60-line PR gets line-by-line scrutiny within an hour, while a 1,500-line PR gets "LGTM" two days later. If you want real review, make PRs small enough that reviewing them properly is cheap. Concretely: separate pure refactors from behaviour changes into different PRs (a diff that is 90% mechanical rename plus 10% logic change hides the 10%), split by layer or by commit, and use **stacked PRs** when a change genuinely cannot be one unit — each PR targets the previous one's branch, and `git rebase --update-refs` keeps the stack coherent when the bottom changes.

**The description is part of the change.** A reviewer needs context you already have and they do not: what problem this solves and why now, what approach you took and what you rejected, how it was tested, what the risk and rollback plan are, and anything you want the reviewer to look at especially hard. Link the issue or incident. Include a screenshot or a log excerpt for anything user-visible. And self-review the diff first, in the web UI — you will catch the leftover debug print, the accidentally committed file, and the unrelated formatting churn before a human wastes their attention on it. Leaving your own inline comments explaining non-obvious choices is one of the cheapest ways to make a PR reviewable.

**Reviewer etiquette is mechanically important, not just polite.** Distinguish blocking from non-blocking explicitly — prefix optional comments with `nit:` and be willing to approve with unresolved nits, because a reviewer who blocks on style is a reviewer people route around. Ask questions rather than issuing commands when you are not certain ("what happens if this map is empty?" surfaces the answer; "add a nil check" may be wrong). Review the code, not the author. And review *fast*: a PR that waits a day goes stale against main, its author has moved on and must reload context, and the whole pipeline slows. Many teams treat review latency as an explicit SLO for exactly this reason.

**Know what the merge buttons actually do.** "Create a merge commit" performs `--no-ff` and preserves your commits. "Squash and merge" creates one new commit whose content is the diff, with a new SHA — which is why the source branch must be deleted afterward and never reused, and why `git branch --merged` will not list it. "Rebase and merge" replays your commits onto the target with new SHAs and no merge commit. Pick one per repository and disable the others; a history with all three mixed in supports none of the downstream workflows cleanly.

**Merge queues exist because "green on my branch" is not "green after merge."** Two PRs can each pass CI against main and still break main once both land — one renames a function, the other adds a caller; one removes a config key, the other starts reading it. This is the semantic-conflict problem, and no amount of textual merging catches it. "Require branches to be up to date before merging" is the crude fix: it forces you to rebase and re-run CI, which serialises merges by hand and does not scale past a handful of PRs a day. A **merge queue** (GitHub merge queue, GitLab merge trains, Bors, Zuul) is the real fix: it builds and tests the *prospective merged result* of the queued PRs, in order, and only fast-forwards main if that combined state passes. Speculative execution lets it test several candidate combinations in parallel, and a failing PR is ejected from the queue without blocking the ones behind it. Being able to explain the failure the queue prevents — not just naming the feature — is the strong answer.

Round this out with the platform controls that make review meaningful: **CODEOWNERS** to route reviews to the people who actually maintain a path (and to require their approval on sensitive directories), required status checks, dismissing stale approvals when new commits are pushed, and requiring signed commits on release branches. Draft PRs signal "not ready" without occupying reviewers, and a `Fixes #123` line closes the issue on merge and keeps the audit trail intact.

sections.title: 19. Monorepos: What Actually Breaks and How Git Copes
sections.content:
A monorepo is one repository containing many independently deployable projects. The reason organisations adopt it is coordination, not storage: one commit can change a service and its client and the shared library between them **atomically**, so there is never a window where the repository describes an inconsistent system. There is exactly one version of every internal dependency, which eliminates diamond-dependency hell, and large-scale refactors (rename an API across 300 call sites) become one reviewable change instead of a six-month migration across 40 repositories. The costs are real and concentrated in tooling.

**Git's slow paths are per-file, not per-byte.** `git status` must decide whether each tracked file changed, and its fast path is an `lstat` per entry plus a scan for untracked files. At 500,000 files that is seconds, every time. The mitigations are all about avoiding those syscalls: `core.untrackedCache` caches directory mtimes so unchanged directories are not rescanned; `core.fsmonitor` (built in for macOS and Windows since Git 2.37, and available via Watchman elsewhere) has the OS tell Git which paths changed since last time, turning the scan into a lookup; and `feature.manyFiles` bundles several of these settings.

**Clone size** is the other wall, and it has three independent axes: number of commits, number of files per commit, and size of file contents. Git's answers map onto those axes. A **shallow clone** (`--depth=1`) truncates history — fast, but it breaks `git merge-base`, `git describe`, and blame, so it suits ephemeral CI jobs and nothing else. A **partial clone** keeps the full commit graph but defers object download: `--filter=blob:none` (blobless) fetches file contents on demand, which keeps history operations working while cutting clone size dramatically; `--filter=tree:0` (treeless) is more aggressive and makes anything that needs trees, including most history traversal, slow. **Sparse-checkout** limits which paths appear in the working tree at all: `git sparse-checkout set --cone services/auth libs/common` gives you those directories plus the root files. Cone mode restricts patterns to whole directories, which lets Git use fast prefix matching rather than evaluating gitignore-style patterns per path, and it enables the **sparse index** — the on-disk index stores a single entry for an excluded directory instead of one entry per file inside it, which is what makes `git status` fast rather than merely making the working tree smaller. `scalar clone` (bundled with Git since 2.38) sets up partial clone, sparse-checkout, the commit-graph, and background maintenance in one command with sensible defaults.

**Binaries are the classic self-inflicted wound.** Git stores every version of every file forever, and binary files do not delta-compress. One 200 MB asset updated weekly for two years is a repository nobody can clone. **Git LFS** solves it with a clean/smudge filter: the committed content is a small text pointer containing an OID and size, and the real bytes live in an LFS server, fetched on checkout. Configured via `.gitattributes`. The important caveat is that LFS must be adopted *before* the binaries land — retrofitting means rewriting history, with all the pain of section 22 — and that LFS adds a hard dependency on a second service, which must be part of your backup and access-control story.

**CI is where monorepos actually fail.** Running the entire test suite on every commit does not scale, so you need to compute the affected set: which targets depend, transitively, on the files this change touched. Build systems with an explicit dependency graph (Bazel, Pants, Buck) do this exactly and cache aggressively; JS-ecosystem tools (Nx, Turborepo) approximate it from package manifests; the cheap version is path filters in your CI config, which is coarse but works surprisingly well early on. Whatever the mechanism, the diff base has to be right — comparing against `origin/main` requires enough history to find the merge base, which is another reason blanket `--depth=1` in CI causes grief.

**Ownership and review** need structure once thousands of people share one repository: CODEOWNERS to route reviews per directory, required approvals on sensitive paths, and a merge queue, which becomes mandatory rather than nice-to-have because merge conflicts and semantic conflicts scale with the number of concurrent merges into one branch.

The honest trade-off summary for an interview: monorepos buy atomic cross-project changes, one dependency version, and easy large-scale refactoring, and they cost you a real investment in build tooling, CI selectivity, and Git scaling work. Polyrepos are cheap on day one and pay the coordination cost forever in version skew and multi-repo pull requests. Neither is universally right; what is wrong is adopting a monorepo without funding the tooling.

# Make a huge working copy usable ------------------------------------------
git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/acme/monorepo.git
cd monorepo
git sparse-checkout set --cone services/auth libs/common
git sparse-checkout list
git sparse-checkout add services/billing
git sparse-checkout disable                # back to a full checkout

# Or let scalar configure all of it (Git 2.38+) ----------------------------
scalar clone https://github.com/acme/monorepo.git
#   -> partial clone + sparse-checkout + commit-graph + background maintenance

# Speed up status / index operations ---------------------------------------
git config core.untrackedCache true
git config core.fsmonitor true             # built-in on macOS/Windows (2.37+)
git config index.version 4                 # path-prefix compression
git config feature.manyFiles true          # bundles several of the above
git maintenance start                      # keep commit-graph & MIDX fresh
git status                                 # measure before/after; it should be ms

# Clone strategies compared -------------------------------------------------
#   --depth=1           tiny+fast   | breaks merge-base, describe, blame
#   --filter=blob:none  small       | full history works; blobs fetched on demand
#   --filter=tree:0     smallest    | history traversal needs network; specialised
#   --sparse            small tree  | fewer files on disk AND (cone) a sparse index

# CI: only test what changed ------------------------------------------------
git fetch --no-tags origin main            # need enough history for a merge base
BASE=$(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)
CHANGED=$(git diff --name-only "$BASE"...HEAD)
echo "$CHANGED" | cut -d/ -f1-2 | sort -u  # naive: affected top-level projects
# Real answer: a build graph.
#   bazel query "rpdeps(//..., set($CHANGED))"     # reverse deps of changed files
#   nx affected --base=$BASE --target=test
#   turbo run test --filter="...[$BASE]"

# Binaries: Git LFS ---------------------------------------------------------
git lfs install
git lfs track "*.psd" "*.mp4" "assets/**/*.bin"
git add .gitattributes
#   .gitattributes gets:
#     *.psd filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
#   The commit stores a ~130-byte pointer:
#     version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1
#     oid sha256:4d7a2...c1
#     size 20481923
git lfs ls-files
git lfs migrate import --include="*.psd" --everything   # retrofit = HISTORY REWRITE

# Find what is bloating the repository -------------------------------------
git count-objects -vH
git rev-list --objects --all \
  | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize:disk) %(rest)' \
  | awk '$1=="blob"' | sort -k3 -n -r | head -20

sections.title: 20. Packfiles, Delta Compression, and Repository Performance
sections.content:
Everything so far has treated objects as individual compressed files, and that is how Git writes them first: a **loose object** per blob, tree, and commit under `.git/objects/ab/cdef...`. Loose objects are simple and safe to write concurrently, but they are terrible at scale — one file per version of every file ever, each compressed in isolation, so a text file with a thousand small revisions costs a thousand nearly-identical compressed copies.

**Packfiles** fix that. `git gc` (or `git repack`) collects loose objects into a single `.pack` file plus an `.idx` index that maps object IDs to offsets. Two things make packs efficient. First, objects are stored **delta-compressed against each other**: Git heuristically groups similar objects (by type, then by path name and size) into a sliding window and stores many of them as a delta against a chosen base, then zlib-compresses the result. `pack.window` (default 10) controls how many candidates are considered and `pack.depth` (default 50) caps how long a delta chain may get — longer chains save space but cost CPU on read, since reconstructing an object means replaying the chain. Second, the pack is a single file, so reading many objects is sequential I/O instead of thousands of small opens.

Crucially, **deltas are a storage-layer detail, not the data model**. Git still conceptually stores whole snapshots; the pack just notices that two snapshots share almost all their bytes. This is the precise answer to the common half-truth "Git stores snapshots, not diffs" — at the object model level yes, at the storage level it absolutely stores diffs, and both statements are true at their own layer.

Three auxiliary structures matter for performance on large repositories. **Reachability bitmaps** (`git repack -b`, or automatically on the server) precompute, for selected commits, a bitmap of every object reachable from them; this turns clone and fetch negotiation from a graph walk into bitwise operations and is a large part of why fetching from a well-maintained server is fast. The **commit-graph** file (`git commit-graph write`, maintained automatically since Git 2.24 via `gc.writeCommitGraph`, and by `git maintenance`) caches commit metadata and **generation numbers** — a topological level per commit — so that `git merge-base`, `git log --graph`, and ancestry checks can prune the walk instead of traversing all of history. The **multi-pack-index** (`git multi-pack-index write`) gives a single lookup structure across many packs, so a repository does not have to be repacked into one giant pack to stay fast.

`git gc` is the porcelain that ties this together: repack loose objects, prune unreachable objects older than `gc.pruneExpire` (default two weeks), expire reflogs, pack refs, and update the commit-graph. It runs opportunistically as `git gc --auto` when loose objects exceed `gc.auto` (default 6700) or packs exceed `gc.autoPackLimit` (default 50). `git maintenance` (Git 2.29+) is the modern replacement: it can be scheduled and runs incremental tasks — incremental repack, commit-graph update, prefetch — that avoid the long stop-the-world repack.

`--aggressive` deserves a caveat because it is widely cargo-culted. It discards existing deltas and recomputes them with a much larger window and depth. On a repository that has never been well packed it can help; on a normally-maintained one it burns a lot of CPU for little gain, and because it throws away the carefully-built delta chains from previous packs it can occasionally make things slightly worse. It is not a routine command.

The production-relevant symptoms: a repository that is slow to clone usually has either a huge number of objects (history depth or file count) or large undeltifiable blobs (binaries), and `git count-objects -vH` plus a sorted list of the biggest blobs will tell you which within a minute. A server that is slow to fetch usually lacks bitmaps or has hundreds of small packs. A client where `git log` is slow usually lacks a commit-graph. And a repository that keeps growing after you deleted the big files is behaving correctly — deletion only stops future versions; the historical blobs remain until history is rewritten.

# What is on disk ----------------------------------------------------------
git count-objects -vH
#   count: 218            <- loose objects
#   size: 1.42 MiB
#   in-pack: 1483920      <- objects inside packfiles
#   packs: 3
#   size-pack: 812.44 MiB
ls .git/objects/pack/     # <name>.pack  <name>.idx  [<name>.bitmap]  [.rev]

# Inspect a pack ------------------------------------------------------------
git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/pack-*.idx | head
#   <sha> blob 4821 1633 12 1 <base-sha>
#     $1    $2   $3   $4  $5 $6    $7
#     sha  type size size-in-pack offset depth base-sha   (depth/base only for deltas)
git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/pack-*.idx \
  | awk '$2=="blob" {print $4, $1}' | sort -n -r | head   # biggest ON DISK

# Maintenance ---------------------------------------------------------------
git gc                                  # normal: respects grace periods
git repack -adb                         # -a all into one pack, -d drop redundant,
                                        # -b write a reachability bitmap
git commit-graph write --reachable      # speeds up log/merge-base/ancestry
git multi-pack-index write              # one index across many packs
git maintenance start                   # scheduled incremental upkeep (2.29+)
git maintenance run --task=incremental-repack

# Tuning knobs (defaults shown) --------------------------------------------
#   pack.window        10     delta candidates considered per object
#   pack.depth         50     max delta chain length (longer = smaller, slower reads)
#   gc.auto            6700   loose objects before `gc --auto` packs
#   gc.autoPackLimit   50     packs before `gc --auto` consolidates
#   gc.pruneExpire     2.weeks.ago
#   core.commitGraph   true
git config pack.threads 0               # 0 = use all cores when packing

# `--aggressive` is not routine --------------------------------------------
git gc --aggressive     # discards existing deltas, recomputes with a big window.
                        # Expensive; only worth it on a badly-packed repo, and
                        # it can undo good delta chains from prior packs.

# Diagnose "why is our clone 4 GB?" ----------------------------------------
git rev-list --objects --all \
 | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize:disk) %(rest)' \
 | awk '$1=="blob"' | sort -k3 -n -r | head -20
#   -> if the top entries are .zip/.mp4/.iso: the fix is LFS + a history
#      rewrite (section 22), not `gc --aggressive`.

sections.title: 21. Tags, Signing, and Release Provenance
sections.content:
Tags are how a repository states "this exact tree is version 1.4.0", and they are the join point between source control and everything downstream: release notes, artefact naming, deployment records, and incident forensics. There are two kinds and the difference matters.

A **lightweight tag** is just a ref under `refs/tags/` pointing at a commit — the same structure as a branch, except Git does not move it when you commit. A **annotated tag** creates an actual **tag object** in the object database containing the target object ID, the tag name, a tagger identity and timestamp, a message, and optionally a GPG or SSH signature; the ref then points at that tag object rather than at the commit. For anything that leaves your machine, use annotated tags (`git tag -a`, or `-s` to sign): you get an author, a date, a message explaining what the release was, and a signable artefact. Lightweight tags are fine as private bookmarks.

Tags are also *not* fetched by the normal branch refspec. Git's default behaviour is to auto-follow tags that point at objects you are already downloading, which is why you usually get them without thinking about it; `git fetch --tags` forces all of them, and `git push --tags` or `git push origin v1.4.0` sends them (a plain `git push` does not). The rule that follows is important operationally: **never move a tag that has been published**. Clients already holding `v1.4.0` will not update it by default, so moving it produces a world where different machines disagree about what `v1.4.0` means — the worst possible failure for a release identifier. If you tagged the wrong commit, publish `v1.4.1`.

`git describe` is the underrated command here. `git describe --tags` produces something like `v1.4.0-17-g9f3c1ab`: the most recent reachable tag, how many commits since, and the abbreviated commit. Building that string into your binary's `--version` output is one of the highest-value things you can do for on-call, because it turns "which code is this?" into an exact answer during an incident. The inverse, `git describe --contains <sha>`, tells you the first tag that contains a given commit — that is, which release shipped it.

**Signing** answers a different question: who authored this, and has it been tampered with? Git supports GPG signing of commits (`commit.gpgsign`) and tags (`git tag -s`), and since Git 2.34 also **SSH signing** (`gpg.format = ssh` with `user.signingkey` pointing at an SSH key), which is dramatically easier to adopt because everyone already has an SSH key and the allowed-signers file is a plain text list. Verification is `git verify-commit`, `git verify-tag`, or `git log --show-signature`.

Be precise about what a signature proves. It proves that the holder of a key produced that object and that its content, including the entire history behind it, is unmodified. It does not prove the code is good, and it does not prove much at all unless someone actually verifies it — an unverified signature is decoration. The meaningful deployment is: a policy requiring signed commits or signed tags on protected branches, enforced by the platform, with an allowed-signers list that is itself managed. Note also that when you merge via a hosting platform's web UI, the resulting merge commit is signed by *the platform*, not by you — which is fine, but it means "all commits on main are signed" means "signed by whoever, including the bot", unless you check the identity too.

Around this sits the broader supply-chain story that interviewers increasingly probe: releases should be reproducible from a tagged commit, the build should record which commit produced which artefact (embed the describe string and the full SHA in the image labels), artefacts should be signed too (Sigstore/cosign is the common answer for containers), and provenance attestations (SLSA) tie the artefact back to the source commit and the builder. Git's contribution to that chain is the tamper-evident hash chain plus signatures; the rest of the chain has to be built on top.

Finally, versioning discipline. Semantic versioning plus **Conventional Commits** lets tooling derive the next version and generate a changelog from commit messages mechanically, which is why `feat:`/`fix:`/`BREAKING CHANGE:` prefixes are worth enforcing in a `commit-msg` hook and in CI. The payoff is not tidy logs; it is that releases stop depending on someone remembering what changed.
