# Lightweight vs annotated --------------------------------------------------
git tag v1.4.0-local                       # lightweight: a ref, nothing else
git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Rate limiting GA"    # annotated: a real tag OBJECT
git tag -s v1.4.0 -m "Rate limiting GA"    # annotated + signed
git cat-file -t v1.4.0                     # "tag" (annotated) vs "commit" (lightweight)
git cat-file -p v1.4.0
#   object 9f3c1ab...
#   type commit
#   tag v1.4.0
#   tagger Alice <alice@example.com> 1786914904 +0530
#
#   Rate limiting GA
#   -----BEGIN SSH SIGNATURE-----

# Publishing ----------------------------------------------------------------
git push origin v1.4.0                     # plain `git push` does NOT send tags
git push origin --tags                     # send them all
git fetch --tags
git tag -d v1.4.0 && git push origin :refs/tags/v1.4.0   # delete (rarely correct)
#   NEVER move a published tag: clients do not update existing tags by
#   default, so v1.4.0 would mean different commits on different machines.
#   Tagged the wrong commit? Ship v1.4.1.

# Provenance you will want at 3am -------------------------------------------
git describe --tags --always --dirty       # v1.4.0-17-g9f3c1ab-dirty
go build -ldflags "-X main.version=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty) \
                   -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
docker build --label org.opencontainers.image.revision=$(git rev-parse HEAD) \
             --label org.opencontainers.image.version=$(git describe --tags) .

# Which release contains this commit? (incident forensics) ------------------
git describe --contains 9f3c1ab            # v1.5.0~12
git tag --contains 9f3c1ab | head
git branch -r --contains 9f3c1ab

# SSH signing: the low-friction option (Git 2.34+) --------------------------
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global tag.gpgsign true
# verification needs an allowed-signers file:
printf 'alice@example.com ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nza...\n' >> ~/.config/git/allowed_signers
git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.config/git/allowed_signers
git log --show-signature -1
git verify-tag v1.4.0
git verify-commit HEAD

# GPG signing ---------------------------------------------------------------
git config --global user.signingkey <KEYID>
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

# What a signature does and does not prove ----------------------------------
#   DOES: this key produced this object; the object and ALL history behind
#         it are unmodified (the hash chain covers ancestors).
#   DOES NOT: mean anyone verified it, or that the code is correct.
#   -> enforce "require signed commits" on protected branches, and remember
#      that web-UI merges are signed by the PLATFORM, not by the author.

sections.title: 22. Secrets in History and Rewriting Published History
sections.content:
Someone commits an AWS key. This is the most common Git-related security incident there is, and interviewers ask about it because the wrong answer — "I did `git rm` and pushed" — reveals a misunderstanding of the object model.

**Order the response correctly, because only one step actually contains the incident: rotate the credential.** The moment a secret reaches a shared remote you must assume it is compromised. Public repositories are scraped continuously by bots that clone, grep, and attempt the credentials within minutes. Even in a private repository, everyone with read access has it, every clone has it, CI caches have it, and backups have it. Removing it from history is *cleanup*; revoking and reissuing it is *containment*. If a candidate leads with `filter-repo`, the follow-up question to ask is "and how long was that key valid for?"

Then understand why deletion is hard. `git rm secrets.env && git commit` removes the file from the *current* tree, but the blob is still in the object database and still reachable from every historical commit that contained it. Anyone can `git show <old-sha>:secrets.env`. To actually remove it you must rewrite every commit from the introducing one to every branch tip — which changes their trees, which changes their hashes, which changes every descendant hash. That is why history rewriting is a big deal: it is not editing one commit, it is republishing the entire graph from that point forward.

The tool to use is **`git filter-repo`** (a separate Python tool, and the one Git's own documentation now recommends), or **BFG Repo-Cleaner** for the simple "delete these paths / replace these strings" cases. `git filter-branch` still exists but is slow, has a long list of correctness footguns, and now prints a warning steering you elsewhere; naming filter-repo instead of filter-branch is a small but real signal. Note that filter-repo intentionally refuses to run on a repository with unpushed changes or existing remotes unless you pass `--force`, and it removes the `origin` remote afterwards — this is deliberate, to stop you from casually force-pushing a rewrite you did not mean to.

Then handle the fallout, which is where the real operational knowledge shows:

- **Every clone must be re-cloned**, or at minimum hard-reset onto the rewritten branches. If anyone merges their old copy back in, the secret returns and so does the duplicated history.
- **Open pull requests break.** Their base commits no longer exist; they must be recreated or rebased with `--onto`.
- **Tags must be rewritten too**, and re-pushed, and consumers who already have them will not update.
- **Forks are outside your control entirely.** A fork retains the old objects, and on GitHub forks share an object store, so the old commit often remains fetchable by SHA from the upstream repository even after your rewrite — the platform has to garbage-collect it, which typically means contacting support. The same applies to `refs/pull/*` refs, which keep PR head commits alive.
- **Caches everywhere**: CI artefacts, container layers, log aggregators, error trackers, chat messages where someone pasted the diff.

All of which reinforces the first point: rotation is the control, rewriting is hygiene.

Prevention is where you should spend most of your answer if the interviewer lets you steer. Layer it: `.gitignore` for the obvious files (`.env`, `*.pem`, `credentials.json`); a **pre-commit secret scanner** (gitleaks, trufflehog, detect-secrets) for fast local feedback; the same scanner in CI so it cannot be bypassed with `--no-verify`; **push protection** on the platform (GitHub secret scanning push protection rejects pushes containing recognised credential formats, which is the closest thing to a real gate on SaaS); and a self-hosted `pre-receive` hook if you run your own server. Above that, remove the reason to have secrets in a repo at all: inject them at runtime from a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, SOPS-encrypted files with KMS, Kubernetes secrets via CSI driver), and prefer short-lived, automatically-rotated credentials (OIDC federation for CI instead of long-lived cloud keys) so that a leak has a short half-life by construction.

One nuance worth mentioning because it shows depth: scanning only new commits in CI is not enough if you have never scanned history — run a full-history scan once, expect false positives from test fixtures, and add allowlists deliberately rather than turning the check off.
sections.code:
# ---- INCIDENT RESPONSE, IN ORDER ----------------------------------------
# 1. ROTATE. Revoke the credential and issue a new one. Everything else is
#    cleanup. Assume the secret is compromised the moment it was pushed.
# 2. Audit for use: cloud audit logs (CloudTrail etc.) for that key id,
#    from the commit's author date to revocation.
# 3. Freeze pushes to the affected branches.
# 4. Then, and only then, clean history.

# Find it -------------------------------------------------------------------
git log --all --full-history -- '**/secrets.env'
git log -S 'AKIA' --oneline --all          # pickaxe: commits changing occurrences
git rev-list --objects --all | grep secrets.env
gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts="--all"

# Rewrite with git-filter-repo (the recommended tool) -----------------------
pip install git-filter-repo
git clone --mirror git@github.com:acme/app.git   # work on a fresh mirror
cd app.git

git filter-repo --invert-paths --path secrets.env            # drop a path everywhere
git filter-repo --invert-paths --path-glob '*.pem'
git filter-repo --path-glob '*.psd' --invert-paths --force

# or redact the string but keep the files:
printf 'AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE==>REDACTED\n' > /tmp/replacements.txt
git filter-repo --replace-text /tmp/replacements.txt

# strip everything over 10MB
git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M

# Push the rewrite ----------------------------------------------------------
git remote add origin git@github.com:acme/app.git   # filter-repo removes remotes on purpose
git push --force --mirror origin      # rewrites ALL refs incl. tags. Coordinate first.

# BFG, for the simple cases -------------------------------------------------
bfg --delete-files secrets.env app.git
bfg --replace-text /tmp/replacements.txt app.git
cd app.git && git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now --aggressive

# What every other clone must do -------------------------------------------
git fetch origin && git reset --hard origin/main
#  ...or just delete the directory and clone again. If ANYONE merges a
#  pre-rewrite branch back in, the secret and the old history return.

# What you cannot fix yourself ---------------------------------------------
#  - forks (separate repos, and on GitHub they share an object store, so the
#    old commit is often still fetchable by SHA from upstream)
#  - refs/pull/<n>/head - PR refs keep old commits alive
#  - CI caches, container layers, log/error aggregators, chat pastes
#  -> ask the hosting provider to garbage-collect, and REMEMBER STEP 1.

# ---- PREVENTION (spend your effort here) ---------------------------------
# .gitignore
.env
.env.*
*.pem
*.p12
credentials.json

# pre-commit framework (.pre-commit-config.yaml)
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.18.4
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

# CI (cannot be skipped with --no-verify)
- run: gitleaks detect --source . --redact --exit-code 1

# Platform: enable secret scanning + PUSH PROTECTION (rejects the push).
# Self-hosted: a pre-receive hook running the same scanner.
# Best of all: no long-lived secrets to leak - OIDC federation for CI,
# short-TTL credentials from a secret manager, SOPS/KMS for config at rest.

sections.title: 23. History Archaeology: Answering 'Why Is This Code Like This?' Under Pressure
sections.content:
Version control's payoff is not storage; it is the ability to reconstruct intent and timeline. During an incident, the questions are always the same: what changed, when did it ship, which release contains it, who understands it, and what was the reasoning. Being fast at this is a genuine SRE skill, and it is a common interview scenario ("the error rate tripled at 14:20 — walk me through what you do in the repo").

**`git log` with the right filters** is the workhorse. `git log --oneline --since='6 hours ago' -- services/auth/` narrows by time and path. `git log --first-parent main` on a merge-based repository gives one entry per integration rather than every intermediate commit. `git log --merges` finds the integrations themselves. `git log v1.4.0..v1.5.0 --oneline` is your release diff, and `--no-merges` cleans it up. Path limiting after `--` is the highest-value habit here: almost every incident is localised to a directory.

**The pickaxe options find where a string entered or left the codebase**, which `git log -- <path>` cannot do. `git log -S'<string>'` shows commits where the *number of occurrences* of that string changed — that is, where it was added or removed — which is how you find when a config key, a magic constant, or a feature flag was introduced. `git log -G'<regex>'` is different and often more useful: it shows commits whose diff text *matches* the regex at all, including moves and modifications that leave the occurrence count unchanged. Say the distinction correctly; interviewers use it as a marker. Add `--pickaxe-all` to see the whole commit rather than only the matching file.

**`git blame` needs its options to be trustworthy.** Bare blame attributes every line to whoever last touched it, which after a reformat or a file move means it attributes everything to the person who ran the formatter. `-w` ignores whitespace changes. `-C` detects lines moved or copied within the file; `-C -C` also looks at files modified in the same commit; `-C -C -C` searches all files in the commit. `-L 40,80` limits to a line range. And `--ignore-rev <sha>` (with `blame.ignoreRevsFile` pointing at a checked-in `.git-blame-ignore-revs`) tells blame to skip bulk-reformat commits permanently — every repository that has ever run a formatter across the tree should have that file, and GitHub honours it too.

Once you have a suspect commit, **turn it into a timeline.** `git describe --contains <sha>` tells you the first tag containing it. `git tag --contains <sha>` and `git branch -r --contains <sha>` tell you everywhere it has spread. `git show <sha>` gives the full change with its message; `git show <sha> --stat` gives the shape first. `git log -1 --format=fuller <sha>` shows both author and committer dates, which reveals whether the commit was rebased or cherry-picked long after it was written — an important detail when correlating with deploy times, because **the commit date is not the deploy time**. The deploy time comes from your CD system; Git only tells you what was in the tree.

**`git log -L`** is the precision instrument most people never learn: `git log -L 40,80:src/limiter.go` shows the complete evolution of that line range, commit by commit, with diffs, following the range as it moves. `git log -L :funcName:file.go` does the same for a function. When the question is "why does this specific block do this", it beats blame because it shows the sequence rather than only the last writer.

Two more habits. **Write commit messages for this moment**, not for the commit list: the subject says what changed, the body says why, what alternative was rejected, and what the risk is; link the ticket or incident. A `git blame` that lands on `fix stuff` is a dead end, and no tooling can recover that information later. And **`.mailmap`** normalises the same human's several email addresses so `git shortlog -sn` and blame do not fragment ownership across "alice@old-company" and "alice@acme".

Finally, know that `git log --follow <file>` exists for renames, that it is a heuristic on top of rename detection and only works for a single path, and that `git log --find-renames` / `-M` controls the similarity threshold. When a file was split into three, no flag will give you a clean answer — you find the commit that did the split with the pickaxe and read it.
sections.code:
# Incident triage: what changed, where, when -------------------------------
git log --oneline --since='6 hours ago' --until='now' -- services/auth/
git log --first-parent --oneline main --since='2 days ago'   # one line per integration
git log --oneline --no-merges v1.4.0..v1.5.0                 # the release diff
git diff v1.4.0..v1.5.0 --stat -- services/auth/
git log --author='@acme.com' --since='1 week' --oneline

# Pickaxe: when did this string arrive or leave? ---------------------------
git log -S'MAX_RETRIES' --oneline --all        # occurrence COUNT changed (add/remove)
git log -G'retry.*backoff' --oneline           # diff TEXT matches the regex (incl. moves)
git log -S'AKIA' --pickaxe-all --all           # show the whole commit, not just the file
#   -S -> "where was it introduced/deleted"    -G -> "where was it touched at all"

# Blame you can trust -------------------------------------------------------
git blame -w -C -C -C -L 40,80 src/limiter.go
#   -w        ignore whitespace-only changes
#   -C        detect moved/copied lines (repeat for wider search)
#   -L a,b    line range
git blame --ignore-rev 1a2b3c4 src/limiter.go        # skip one reformat commit

# Make the reformat commits invisible to blame, forever --------------------
printf '# gofmt sweep 2026-03\n1a2b3c4d5e6f7890abcdef1234567890abcdef12\n' \
  > .git-blame-ignore-revs
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
#   commit that file; GitHub honours it in the web blame view too.

# Evolution of one block or function ---------------------------------------
git log -L 40,80:src/limiter.go
git log -L :refillTokens:src/limiter.go
git log --follow --oneline -- src/new/path/limiter.go     # across a rename

# From a suspect commit to a release timeline ------------------------------
git show 9f3c1ab --stat
git show 9f3c1ab
git log -1 --format=fuller 9f3c1ab      # AuthorDate vs CommitDate: was it rebased?
git describe --contains 9f3c1ab         # first tag containing it -> v1.5.0~12
git tag --contains 9f3c1ab
git branch -r --contains 9f3c1ab        # which release branches carry it
#   NOTE: commit date != deploy time. Correlate with your CD system's record
#   of which SHA was rolled out when.

# Ownership -----------------------------------------------------------------
git shortlog -sn --no-merges -- services/auth/     # who works here (ask them)
git log --format='%an' -- services/auth/ | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
# .mailmap so one human is one name:
#   Alice Kumar <alice@acme.com> <alice@old-company.com>

# Find a commit you half-remember ------------------------------------------
git log --all --grep='rate limit' --oneline
git log --all --oneline -- '**/limiter*'
git rev-list --all | xargs git grep -l 'refillTokens' | head   # slow, but thorough

interviewQA.q: Explain Git's object model. What are the four object types and how do they relate?
interviewQA.a:
Git is a content-addressed key-value store. There are four object types. A blob holds the raw bytes of a file and nothing else - no name, no permissions, no timestamp. A tree is a directory listing: a sorted set of entries, each being a mode, a name, and the object ID of a blob or another tree. A commit points at exactly one tree - the full snapshot of the project - plus zero or more parent commits, an author, a committer, and a message. An annotated tag object points at another object and carries a tagger, a message, and optionally a signature.

Every object is stored identically: Git prepends a header of the type name, a space, the byte length, and a NUL, hashes header-plus-content with SHA-1, and that hash is the object's name. You can reproduce it exactly with `printf 'blob 6\0hello\n' | shasum`, which gives the same ID as `git hash-object`.

Three consequences matter. Identical content is stored once, so unchanged files across a thousand commits are one blob - that is why full snapshots per commit are affordable. Because blobs have no name, Git does not track renames, it detects them at diff time by content similarity, which is why rename detection has a threshold and why a rename plus a heavy edit shows as delete-plus-add. And because a commit's hash covers its tree and its parents, it transitively covers all history behind it, which is why Git is tamper-evident and why editing an old commit necessarily changes every descendant ID - the mechanical reason rebasing produces new commits rather than modifying old ones.
followUps: If Git stores full snapshots, why isn't the repository enormous?
Where do file permissions and filenames actually live, given that a blob has neither?
SHA-1 is broken. Is that a problem for Git, and what has Git done about it?
How would you find the ten largest objects in a repository?

interviewQA.q: What actually happens, at the file level, when you create a branch and commit on it?
interviewQA.a:
Creating a branch writes one file: `.git/refs/heads/<name>` containing the 40-hex object ID of the current commit. That is 41 bytes, and it is O(1) no matter how large the repository is - nothing is copied. (Once there are many refs, Git compacts them into `.git/packed-refs`, and newer versions can use a reftable backend, but the model is the same.)

Switching to it rewrites `.git/HEAD` to contain `ref: refs/heads/<name>`. HEAD is a symbolic ref - a pointer to a pointer - and that indirection is what makes committing work. `git commit` builds a tree from the index, writes a commit object whose parent is the commit HEAD currently resolves to, and then updates whatever ref HEAD points at to the new commit. The branch advances because HEAD is attached to it.

If instead HEAD holds a raw object ID - which happens when you check out a commit, a tag, or a remote-tracking ref - you are in detached HEAD. You can still commit, but no ref follows you, so those commits become unreachable from any branch as soon as you check out something else, findable only through the reflog until it expires. Detached HEAD is not an error; bisect and CI use it deliberately. It is just a state where new work is one careless checkout from being invisible.

The corollary interviewers are usually driving at: a branch is not a container of commits, it is a movable label. The commits "on" a branch are simply those reachable by walking parent pointers from that label, which is why two branches share history by pointing into the same object graph rather than by duplicating anything.
followUps: What is the difference between `git switch` and `git checkout`, and why was the split made?
How does Git decide whether a commit is garbage-collectable?
What is ORIG_HEAD and who writes it?
Why does `git branch --merged` sometimes fail to list a branch whose code is clearly in main?

interviewQA.q: Merge or rebase? When do you use each?
interviewQA.a:
The one non-negotiable rule is: rebase private history, merge public history. Commits nobody else has are yours to reshape; commits on a shared branch must only be appended to, because rewriting them forces every other clone to reconcile two versions of the same work - and the instinctive fix, `git pull`, merges the old copies back in and duplicates everything.

Beyond that it is a team policy, and I would argue for enforcing one policy per repository rather than deciding per PR. Merge preserves what actually happened: nothing is rewritten, and `git log --first-parent main` reads as one entry per feature. The cost is a noisy graph and that `git bisect` can step into mid-feature commits that were never meant to build. Rebase-and-fast-forward gives a strictly linear history where every commit on main has one parent, which makes bisect, blame, and file history maximally simple - but it demands authors who curate their branch, and the chronology is fictional. Squash-merge collapses each PR into one commit, so main becomes a sequence of atomic, revertable units at PR granularity, at the cost of intra-PR blame detail.

The way I choose is to name the property I want main to have: every commit is independently buildable and independently revertable. Squash gets that nearly free and suits application repositories; rebase-and-FF gets it with finer granularity and suits repos where individual commits are genuinely atomic; merge commits suit teams whose branch history is itself an audit artefact.

Whichever you pick, enforce it in the platform - disable the other merge buttons, require linear history if relevant - because a repository with all three enabled produces a history that serves none of the downstream workflows well.

interviewQA.q: What is a three-way merge, and what does the recursive/ort strategy add on top of it?
interviewQA.a:
A two-way comparison cannot merge: if your file says `timeout = 30` and mine says `60`, there is no way to know who changed it. The missing input is the merge base - the best common ancestor of the two commits. With base, ours, and theirs, each hunk can be decided: if only one side differs from base, take that side; if both sides made the same change, take it once; if both changed the same region differently, that is a conflict, and Git writes markers and leaves three versions in the index as stages 1, 2, and 3.

What recursive - and its modern replacement ort - adds is handling for the case where there is more than one merge base. That happens with criss-cross history, where two branches have merged each other in both directions. Rather than arbitrarily picking one ancestor, Git recursively merges the merge bases together into a synthetic virtual base and three-way merges against that. It also does rename detection and directory-rename detection so a file edited on one side and moved on the other merges correctly.

`ort` became the default two-head strategy in Git 2.34. It is a reimplementation that operates on in-memory trees instead of repeatedly rewriting the on-disk index, which makes it much faster - especially on rebases, which are many merges in a row - and fixed a set of rename and directory-rename corner cases. Same algorithm conceptually, much better implementation.

The limitation worth volunteering: this is all textual and structural. A merge can be perfectly clean and still break the build, because one side renamed a function and the other added a caller. Git has no way to see that, which is the entire reason merge queues exist.

interviewQA.q: Explain the difference between `git reset --soft`, `--mixed`, and `--hard`.
interviewQA.a:
All three move the current branch pointer to the target commit. They differ in how much else they touch, and the model to hold is the three trees: HEAD, the index, and the working tree.

`--soft` moves the branch pointer only. The index and working tree are untouched, so everything that was in those commits is now sitting staged relative to the new HEAD. That is the basis of squashing by hand: `git reset --soft HEAD~3 && git commit`.

`--mixed`, the default, moves the pointer and resets the index to match, leaving the working tree alone. Your changes become unstaged modifications. Nothing on disk is lost.

`--hard` moves the pointer, resets the index, and overwrites the working tree. It is the only variant that can destroy work, and it does so with no confirmation and no undo for anything that was never staged or committed.

Two related forms people conflate with these. `git reset <paths>` with no mode flag does not move HEAD at all - it copies those paths from HEAD into the index, which is unstaging; the modern spelling is `git restore --staged <paths>`. And `git restore <paths>` copies from the index into the working tree, discarding unstaged edits.

On recovery: after a bad `--hard`, `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` or `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` gets committed work back, because the commits are unreferenced rather than deleted. What cannot come back is anything never added to Git - uncommitted, unstaged edits. Though if you had run `git add` at any point, the blob is in the object database and `git fsck --lost-found` can recover the content even without a commit.

interviewQA.q: A colleague force-pushed over main and three hours of work is gone. Walk me through it.
interviewQA.a:
First, stop the bleeding: freeze pushes to main and tell everyone not to re-clone and not to run `git gc`. The objects still exist somewhere, and a fresh clone is how you lose the last copy.

Second, find the pre-force SHA. Remote-tracking refs have reflogs, so on any machine that fetched before the force-push, `git reflog show origin/main` shows the old tip. Any developer who had pulled recently is a viable source. Restore with `git push --force-with-lease origin <good-sha>:main`. If the force-push also lost commits that only existed locally for someone, their own `git reflog` has them.

Third, if no local copy survives, go to the host. On GitHub the events API records the before and after SHAs of every push, and objects generally remain fetchable by SHA until the server garbage-collects, so `git fetch origin <sha>` often still works. GitLab has equivalent activity data. This is time-sensitive.

Fourth, prevention, because this is really a process failure. Branch protection on main and on `release/*` should block force-pushes and deletions outright - no one should be able to do this. Individually, configure `push.useForceIfIncludes = true` and always use `--force-with-lease --force-if-includes` rather than `--force`.

Worth explaining the distinction: `--force-with-lease` checks the remote against your remote-tracking ref, but any background fetch - an IDE, a shell prompt - silently updates that ref and disarms the safety. `--force-if-includes` additionally requires that the remote's current tip is reachable from your reflog, meaning you actually saw and integrated it. That closes the hole.

interviewQA.q: How does `git bisect` work, and how would you automate it for a regression that only reproduces intermittently?
interviewQA.a:
Bisect binary-searches the commit graph. You mark one commit bad and one good; Git checks out a midpoint in detached HEAD, you judge it, and the candidate set halves. Roughly log2(N) tests - about ten for a thousand commits.

Automation is `git bisect run <script>`, and the contract is exit-code based: 0 means good, 1 to 127 except 125 means bad, 125 means "cannot test this commit" and is equivalent to skip, and anything else - 128 to 255 - aborts the bisect. Getting 125 right is what separates a working automated bisect from a wrong answer, because in a merge-based history plenty of commits will not build and must not be scored as bad.

For intermittent reproduction, binary search's assumption of a deterministic oracle is violated, and a single flaky result sends the search down the wrong half permanently. I would do three things. First, try to make the reproducer deterministic - pin seeds, fake the clock, remove network dependencies - because that is a cheaper fix than fighting statistics. If I cannot, run the test N times in the script and only report good if all N pass, which biases errors toward "bad"; that is the safe direction, since a false good prunes the half containing the real culprit whereas a false bad only costs an extra step. Third, keep `git bisect log` so that if the result looks implausible I can edit the transcript and `git bisect replay` it rather than starting over.

Two more practical points: the script must live outside the repository, because bisect replaces the working tree at every step; and the script must own its environment - install dependencies or run inside a container - because six-month-old code will not build against today's toolchain.

interviewQA.q: Someone pushed an AWS access key to a repository. What do you do?
interviewQA.a:
Rotate the key first. That is the only step that actually contains the incident. Once a secret reaches a shared remote you must assume it is compromised - public repos are scraped within minutes, and even in a private repo every clone, CI cache, and backup now has it. Revoke and reissue, then check the cloud audit log for use of that key ID between the commit's author date and revocation. Everything after this is cleanup, not containment.

Then understand why removal is hard. `git rm` plus a commit only changes the current tree; the blob is still reachable from every historical commit that contained it, so `git show <old-sha>:secrets.env` still works. Removing it means rewriting every commit from the introducing one to every tip, which changes their trees, hence their hashes, hence every descendant hash. The tool is `git filter-repo` - the one Git's own docs recommend, replacing `filter-branch` - or BFG for the simple "delete this path / redact this string" case. Work on a fresh mirror, then `git push --force --mirror` after coordinating with the team.

Then the fallout, which is the part people forget. Every clone must be re-cloned or hard-reset, or someone merges a pre-rewrite branch and the secret returns. Open PRs break because their base commits no longer exist. Tags must be rewritten and republished. Forks are outside your control - on GitHub forks share an object store, so the old commit is often still fetchable by SHA from upstream until the platform garbage-collects, which usually means asking support. And `refs/pull/*` refs keep PR heads alive.

Prevention is where the effort belongs: gitleaks in a pre-commit hook for fast feedback, the same scan in CI so `--no-verify` cannot bypass it, platform push protection which actually rejects the push, and above all removing the reason for long-lived secrets - OIDC federation for CI, short-TTL credentials from a secret manager, SOPS or KMS for config at rest.

interviewQA.q: Compare `git cherry-pick`, `git revert`, and `git reset`.
interviewQA.a:
They answer three different questions.

`git cherry-pick <c>` applies the change introduced by one commit onto your current branch as a new commit. Mechanically it is a three-way merge with the picked commit's parent as base, so it can conflict like any merge. It preserves the original author but produces a new SHA. The production use is backporting a hotfix to a release branch, and it should always be run with `-x`, which records "(cherry picked from commit ...)" - six months later that line is the only link between the two copies.

`git revert <c>` computes the inverse patch and commits it forward. Nothing is rewritten, so it is safe on public branches, and the history honestly records that the change happened and was undone. This is what you use in production.

`git reset` moves the branch pointer, discarding commits from that branch's reachability. It rewrites history, so it belongs to private branches only.

The rule of thumb: revert for anything anyone else has, reset for your own local history, cherry-pick to move a change between lines of development.

The trap worth raising unprompted is reverting a merge. A merge has two parents so you must say which mainline to keep: `git revert -m 1 <merge>`. That correctly removes the code, but the merge commit remains reachable, so Git still considers the branch merged. When the team later re-merges that branch, the merge base already includes those commits and nothing comes back - "I merged and my code is missing". The fixes are to revert the revert before re-merging, or to redo the work on a fresh branch. Prevention is to squash-merge features, so a revert is one ordinary commit, or to ship behind a flag so rollback is a config change.

interviewQA.q: What is the reflog, and what can it not recover?
interviewQA.a:
A reflog is a per-ref, append-only log of every value that ref has held on this machine. `.git/logs/HEAD` records every HEAD movement; each branch has its own under `.git/logs/refs/heads/`. Each entry records old ID, new ID, who, when, and which command caused it. It is local and per-clone - never pushed, never fetched, and absent in a fresh clone.

It works because Git does not delete commits; it stops referencing them. So after `git reset --hard HEAD~3`, those three commits are still in the object database and the reflog still names the old tip: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` brings them back. `ORIG_HEAD`, which reset, merge, rebase, and pull all write before moving HEAD, is the one-step version.

Note that `HEAD@{2}` is reflog syntax - where HEAD was two moves ago in time - not ancestry syntax like `HEAD~2`. They usually point at completely different commits.

What it cannot recover is anything that was never in the object database. Uncommitted, unstaged working-tree edits destroyed by `reset --hard` or `checkout -- <file>` are gone. `git clean -fdx` deletes untracked files, which were never objects - gone. Ignored files - gone. Also anything on someone else's machine, since reflogs are not shared, and anything at all after garbage collection has actually run past the expiry windows: 90 days for reachable reflog entries, 30 days for unreachable ones, and a two-week grace on unreachable loose objects.

One useful nuance: if you ever ran `git add`, the blob was written to the object database at that moment. So even with no commit and no reflog entry, `git fsck --lost-found` can recover the file content - you just have to identify it by grepping the dangling blobs.

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`, and why do people say to avoid `pull`?
interviewQA.a:
`git fetch` downloads objects and updates your remote-tracking refs under `refs/remotes/origin/*`, following the refspec `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*`. It changes nothing about your branches, your index, or your working tree, so it cannot lose work. Those tracking refs are a cache: `origin/main` means "main as of my last fetch", not "main right now".

`git pull` is fetch plus an integration step - merge by default, or rebase if configured. The objection is not that pull is broken; it is that the integration happens before you have looked at what arrived. With the default, a divergent branch silently gains a "Merge branch 'main' of ..." commit that nobody intended, and on a shared branch those accumulate into an unreadable graph. Since Git 2.27 Git warns when a pull would need to reconcile divergent branches with no strategy configured, precisely to push people into making the choice explicitly.

What I actually configure is `pull.ff = only`. Then a pull either fast-forwards cleanly or stops and tells me the branches diverged, at which point I decide: `git rebase origin/main` for a topic branch I own, `git merge origin/main` for a shared one. Teams that prefer a linear history can instead set `pull.rebase = true`, which is fine as long as everyone understands it rewrites their local commits.

The habit worth stating: fetch, look (`git log HEAD..origin/main --oneline`, `git diff HEAD...origin/main`), then integrate. It costs one extra command and eliminates a whole class of surprise.

interviewQA.q: Your PR is green and main is green, but main breaks right after your PR merges. How is that possible and how do you prevent it?
interviewQA.a:
Because CI tested your branch against an older main, not against the state that results from merging. Two PRs can each be green independently and still break when combined - one renames a function while the other adds a call to the old name, or one deletes a config key while the other starts reading it. There is no textual conflict, so the merge is clean and the build is broken. That is a semantic conflict, and Git structurally cannot detect it: it merges text and tree structure, not meaning.

The crude fix is "require branches to be up to date before merging", which forces you to rebase onto current main and re-run CI. It works, but it serialises merges by hand - every merge invalidates everyone else's up-to-date status - so it collapses beyond a handful of merges a day.

The real fix is a merge queue: GitHub merge queue, GitLab merge trains, Bors, or Zuul. Instead of testing your branch, the queue constructs the prospective merged result of the queued PRs in order and tests that. Main only fast-forwards if the combined state passes. Good implementations speculate - testing several candidate combinations in parallel - so throughput does not collapse, and a failing PR is ejected without blocking the ones behind it.

Two supporting practices. Short-lived branches, because the probability of a semantic conflict scales with how far your branch has drifted from main. And post-merge CI on main with an automatic revert or rollback path, because no gate is perfect and the recovery time matters more than the incident rate.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through resolving a nasty merge conflict. What does the tooling actually give you?
interviewQA.a:
First, know what a conflict is: during the three-way merge, both sides changed the same region relative to the merge base, and changed it differently. Underneath, the index holds three entries for that path - stage 1 base, stage 2 ours, stage 3 theirs - and the file on disk is a rendering of them. That is why `git add <file>` is what marks it resolved: it collapses the three stages into one.

The single highest-value setting is `merge.conflictStyle = zdiff3` (or diff3). The default style shows only ours and theirs, so you have to guess what the original was. diff3 shows the base too, which converts the question from "which of these two do I like" into "what did each side actually change", and that is usually the difference between resolving correctly and resolving plausibly. zdiff3 is the same information with common lines hoisted out of the conflict block.

My working loop: `git status` and `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U` to see the scope, then for each file `git log --merge -p <file>` to see only the commits from both sides that touched it - that recovers intent, which is what you need. Then resolve semantically; the correct output is often neither side verbatim but the code that satisfies both intentions. Then build and run the tests before committing the merge, always.

Two gotchas worth stating. `--ours` and `--theirs` invert during a rebase, because Git checks out the upstream and replays your commits onto it - so "ours" is the branch you are rebasing onto and "theirs" is your own commit. Blindly taking `--ours` in a rebase throws away your work. And some files should never be merged textually: mark lockfiles and generated files with `-merge` in `.gitattributes` so Git always conflicts, then resolve by regenerating rather than by hand-splicing two machine-generated files into something that parses but is wrong.

For repeated conflicts - a long rebase, or a branch you keep merging main into - `rerere.enabled = true` records each resolution and replays it automatically. Enormous time saver, with the caveat that it will faithfully replay a wrong resolution forever until you `git rerere forget`.

interviewQA.q: How do you keep a very large monorepo workable for both developers and CI?
interviewQA.a:
Split the problem by what is actually slow: number of commits, number of files, size of file contents, and CI breadth.

For clone size, partial clone is usually the right tool: `--filter=blob:none` keeps the full commit graph so history, merge-base, and blame still work, but fetches file contents lazily. Shallow clones (`--depth=1`) are faster still but break `git describe`, `merge-base`, and blame, so I would keep them to throwaway CI jobs. For working-tree size, `git sparse-checkout set --cone <dirs>` gives a developer only the directories they work in; cone mode matters because it restricts patterns to whole directories, which lets Git use prefix matching and enables the sparse index - an excluded directory becomes one index entry instead of thousands, which is what actually makes `git status` fast. `scalar clone` configures partial clone, sparse-checkout, commit-graph, and background maintenance in one go.

For local operations, the cost is per-file syscalls, so enable `core.untrackedCache` and `core.fsmonitor` (built in on macOS and Windows since 2.37) and let `git maintenance` keep the commit-graph and multi-pack-index fresh.

For binaries, Git LFS - the commit stores a small pointer and the bytes live in an LFS server. Critically, adopt it before the binaries land; retrofitting requires a history rewrite.

For CI, the whole game is computing the affected set. A build system with a real dependency graph (Bazel, Pants) answers "what depends on these files" exactly; Nx or Turborepo approximate it from package manifests; path filters are the cheap version. Make sure the diff base is correct - you need enough history to compute a merge base against main, which is another argument against blanket shallow clones.

And organisationally: CODEOWNERS to route review by directory, plus a merge queue, which becomes mandatory rather than optional because conflict probability scales with the number of concurrent merges into one branch.

interviewQA.q: How do submodules work, and what goes wrong with them in practice?
interviewQA.a:
A submodule is a tree entry with mode 160000 - a gitlink - whose object ID is a commit SHA that does not exist in this repository. Alongside it, the tracked `.gitmodules` file maps that path to a URL. So the superproject records "at this path, I depend on exactly this commit of that other repo", and nothing else.

Everything that goes wrong follows from that design. Cloning the superproject does not populate the submodule - you get an empty directory until `git submodule update --init --recursive`, or you cloned with `--recurse-submodules`. The pin is a bare commit ID with no branch, so submodule checkouts are detached HEAD by default, and work committed inside one is easy to orphan.

The most common outage is push order. If you commit in the child, commit the updated gitlink in the parent, and push only the parent, everyone else and CI get a gitlink pointing at a commit that does not exist on the remote - "fatal: reference is not a tree". Always push the child first, or use `git push --recurse-submodules=on-demand`, and set `push.recurseSubmodules = check` so Git refuses the push otherwise.

Beyond that: merges can conflict on the gitlink itself, which presents as two commit IDs and no text, so you have to decide which child commit is correct and `git add` the path. Everyone who clones needs read access to every submodule repo, which becomes an onboarding and CI-credentials problem. And branch switching in the parent does not move the submodule unless `submodule.recurse` is set.

So I would use them narrowly: when I need a Git-native pin to an exact commit of a repository I do not control. For third-party code with releases, a package registry gives me versioning, checksums, and transitive resolution that submodules approximate badly. For tightly-coupled internal code, a monorepo. `git subtree` sits in between - it copies the content into your tree, so a plain clone just works and CI needs nothing special, at the cost of repository growth and clunkier upstream contribution.

interviewQA.q: How would you enforce that every commit reaching main passes lint, has a valid commit message, and contains no secrets?
interviewQA.a:
The key framing is that client-side hooks are feedback and server-side controls are policy. A pre-commit hook is skipped by `git commit --no-verify` or by deleting the file, so anything that must hold cannot live only there.

I would layer it. Locally, versioned hooks: commit a `.githooks/` directory and set `core.hooksPath` to it, or use husky, lefthook, or the pre-commit framework so it installs automatically. `pre-commit` runs the linter over staged files only and a secret scanner; `commit-msg` validates the Conventional Commits format. The design constraint is speed - budget a second or two, because a fifteen-second pre-commit hook trains the entire team to type `--no-verify`, and then you have negative value. Anything slower goes in `pre-push`.

Then the enforcement layer. On a self-hosted server, a `pre-receive` hook: it receives all ref updates on stdin, and a non-zero exit rejects the whole push atomically. That is where I would put secret scanning, maximum file size, protected-path rules, and required commit-message format. On github.com you cannot install pre-receive, so the equivalent is branch protection plus required status checks: require a PR, require the lint/test/gitleaks checks to pass, require CODEOWNERS approval on sensitive paths, block force-push and deletion, and enable secret-scanning push protection, which is the closest thing to a genuine push-time gate on SaaS.

Then CI runs the same checks again, because that is the copy nobody can skip, and it is the check the branch protection rule actually depends on.

One implementation detail worth mentioning: a pre-commit hook that auto-formats writes to the working tree, but the commit is built from the index, so the formatted version is not what gets committed unless the hook re-stages - and re-staging blindly can sweep in unrelated unstaged changes. Safer to fail the commit with a clear message than to silently mutate the developer's tree.

interviewQA.q: What makes a good pull request, from both the author's and the reviewer's side?
interviewQA.a:
From the author: size first, everything else second. Review quality drops sharply as diffs grow - the commonly cited industry data puts effective review in the low hundreds of lines per hour with defect detection falling off well before four hundred lines - and the behavioural effect is stronger than the statistical one. A 60-line PR gets line-by-line scrutiny within the hour; a 1,500-line PR gets "LGTM" two days later. Concretely that means splitting pure refactors from behaviour changes, because a diff that is 90% mechanical rename hides the 10% that matters, and using stacked PRs when a change genuinely cannot be one unit.

Second, the description is part of the change: what problem this solves and why now, what approach you took and what you rejected, how it was tested, the risk and the rollback plan, and where you want the reviewer to look hardest. Link the ticket or incident. Then self-review the diff in the web UI before requesting review - that catches the debug print and the accidental file - and leave inline comments explaining non-obvious decisions.

From the reviewer: separate blocking from non-blocking explicitly, prefix optional comments with "nit:", and be willing to approve with unresolved nits, because a reviewer who blocks on style is one people route around. Ask questions rather than issue commands when you are not sure - "what happens if this map is empty?" surfaces the answer, whereas "add a nil check" might be wrong. Review the code, not the author. And review promptly: a PR that waits a day goes stale against main and its author has to reload context, so review latency is worth treating as a team SLO.

The mechanical piece that supports all of this: pick one merge method and disable the others, auto-delete head branches (essential with squash-merge), require CODEOWNERS approval on sensitive paths, and dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed.

interviewQA.q: What's in the Git index, and why is `git status` slow in a huge repository?
interviewQA.a:
The index - `.git/index`, also called the staging area or cache - is a binary file containing one sorted entry per tracked path. Each entry has the path, the file mode, the blob ID of the staged content, and a cache of the file's stat data at the time Git last looked: device, inode, ctime, mtime, size, uid, gid. It is a flat manifest of a proposed next commit, not a list of diffs.

Two things follow. First, `git add` writes the blob into the object database immediately - the content is durable in `.git/objects` before you ever commit, which is why `git fsck --lost-found` can recover staged-but-never-committed work. Second, `git status` does not hash your files. It `lstat`s each entry and compares size and mtime against the cached values, hashing only when they differ. That is why it is normally instantaneous.

Which is exactly why it is slow at scale: with 500,000 tracked files it is 500,000 syscalls plus a full directory walk to find untracked files, every single time. The mitigations all attack the syscall count. `core.untrackedCache` caches directory mtimes so unchanged directories are skipped. `core.fsmonitor` - built in for macOS and Windows since Git 2.37, Watchman elsewhere - has the OS report which paths changed, turning the scan into a lookup. And sparse-checkout in cone mode enables the sparse index, where an excluded directory occupies a single index entry rather than one per file, which shrinks the index itself rather than just the working tree.

Two related details: the index also holds up to three versions of a path during a conflict - stages 1, 2, and 3 for base, ours, and theirs - which is how `git checkout --ours` knows what to give you. And the stat-cache design is why `--assume-unchanged` and `--skip-worktree` exist, and why people who use them to hide local config edits end up debugging "my change silently disappeared".

interviewQA.q: You have a branch with 12 messy commits. How do you turn it into something reviewable, and how do you prove each commit builds?
interviewQA.a:
`git rebase -i origin/main` opens a todo list, one line per commit, oldest first, and Git executes whatever I leave there. I reorder by moving lines, drop by deleting them, and change the action verb: `reword` to fix a message, `squash` to combine and merge the messages, `fixup` to combine and discard the message, `edit` to stop and do surgery.

In practice I do not build that list by hand. While working, when I notice a mistake belonging to an earlier commit, I commit it as `git commit --fixup=<sha>`, which produces a `fixup! <subject>` message. Then `git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main` automatically reorders those commits next to their targets and pre-marks them as fixups, so I usually just save and quit. Setting `rebase.autoSquash = true` makes that the default. This is also how review feedback should be folded in, rather than leaving a trail of "address review comments" commits.

Splitting a commit is a fixed recipe worth memorising: mark it `edit`; when the rebase stops, `git reset HEAD^` to un-commit while keeping the changes in the working tree; then `git add -p` and commit in logical pieces; then `git rebase --continue`.

To prove each commit builds, `git rebase -i --exec 'make build && make test' origin/main` inserts an `exec` after every commit in the range and halts at the first failure. If the team's policy is "every commit on main is buildable" - which is what makes bisect and revert reliable - that is how you actually verify it instead of hoping. It is slow, so I run it once before pushing the finished stack.

Then `git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes`, and I tell reviewers I rebased, because a force-push invalidates in-flight comments on the old commits.

interviewQA.q: Explain trunk-based development. Why does branch lifetime matter so much?
interviewQA.a:
Trunk-based development means everyone integrates into a single trunk at least daily, branches live hours rather than days, incomplete work ships to production disabled behind feature flags rather than being held back on a branch, and release branches - if they exist at all - are cut from trunk purely for stabilisation, with fixes cherry-picked from trunk rather than developed on the branch.

The reason lifetime is the variable is that integration is where risk concentrates: it is the moment when independently-made assumptions collide. Deferring integration does not reduce that risk, it batches it, and batched risk arrives all at once at the worst possible time - just before a release, from several authors who have paged out the context. Conflicts also grow with divergence, and not just textual ones: semantic conflicts, where a merge is clean but the build breaks because one side renamed something the other started calling, become much more likely the further your branch has drifted. And CI signal degrades - green on a branch two hours behind trunk means something, green on a branch two weeks behind means very little.

The DORA research consistently associates trunk-based development and short-lived branches with high delivery performance, which is the empirical version of the same argument.

The honest cost is feature flags. A flag is a runtime branch, so code paths multiply, tests have to cover the combinations that will actually exist in production, and stale flags accumulate. Without a flag lifecycle - an owner and a removal date per flag, an audit of old ones, deletion after full rollout - you have simply traded merge debt for flag debt, which is harder to see.

Contrast with GitFlow, which has `develop` and `master` plus release and hotfix branches. It genuinely solved shipping versioned, installed software with several supported releases; Driessen himself later added a note saying it is not the right model for continuously-delivered web applications. My answer to "which model" is conditional: continuously-deployed service, trunk-based with flags; mobile or on-prem with real release trains, trunk plus release branches; small team on a web app, GitHub Flow. And encode whichever it is in branch protection rules, not in a wiki page.

interviewQA.q: How would you find which commit introduced a subtle behaviour change, when you don't have a failing test?
interviewQA.a:
I would work from three directions and use whichever narrows fastest.

Path and time filtering first, because it is nearly free: `git log --oneline --since='2 days ago' -- services/auth/`. On a merge-based repository `--first-parent` gives one entry per integration rather than every intermediate commit, which is usually the right resolution for "what shipped".

Then the pickaxe, which finds things `git log -- <path>` cannot. `git log -S'<string>'` shows commits where the number of occurrences of that string changed - that is, where it was introduced or removed - so it finds when a config key, constant, or flag first appeared. `git log -G'<regex>'` is different: it matches the diff text at all, so it also catches modifications and moves that leave the count unchanged. Knowing which of the two to reach for is most of the skill.

For a specific block of code, `git log -L 40,80:src/limiter.go` or `git log -L :funcName:file.go` shows the full evolution of that range with diffs, following it as it moves. That beats blame when the question is "why does this do this", because blame only tells you who touched it last.

Blame itself needs its options: `-w` to ignore whitespace, `-C -C -C` to follow moved and copied lines, and a checked-in `.git-blame-ignore-revs` with `blame.ignoreRevsFile` set, so bulk reformat commits do not attribute the whole file to whoever ran the formatter.

If I can turn the behaviour into any boolean predicate - even a manual "does this look wrong" - then `git bisect` beats all of this, because it is logarithmic rather than linear in the number of candidate commits, and the predicate does not have to be a test suite.

Once I have a suspect: `git show`, then `git describe --contains <sha>` to find the first release containing it, `git tag --contains` and `git branch -r --contains` to see where it spread, and `git log -1 --format=fuller` to check whether author and commit dates differ, which tells me it was rebased or cherry-picked and that the commit date is not the deploy time.

interviewQA.q: What does `git stash` actually create, and when would you use something else?
interviewQA.a:
Stash creates commits. `git stash push` writes a commit for your current index state, then a commit for your working tree whose first parent is HEAD and whose second parent is that index commit, and with `-u` a third parent holding untracked files. It points `refs/stash` at the working-tree commit and resets your tree back to HEAD. You can see all of this with `git cat-file -p refs/stash`. The "stack" is `refs/stash` plus its reflog, which is why `stash@{2}` is reflog syntax and why dropped stashes remain recoverable via `git fsck` until garbage collection.

The pitfalls follow from that. Untracked files are not included by default, which is how people lose work: stash, then `git clean -fd` to get a pristine tree, and the clean deletes exactly the files the stash did not save - and since they were never objects, nothing recovers them. `pop` is `apply` plus `drop` and only drops if the apply succeeded, so a conflicted pop leaves the entry behind and people later pop it twice. And `apply` flattens your staged/unstaged split unless you pass `--index`.

The bigger point is that a stash is not a branch and not a backup: local-only, invisible in `git status`, unnamed unless you pass `-m`, and easy to accumulate. Anything I will not resume within an hour goes into a WIP commit on a branch instead - visible, named, pushable, and safe.

And for the most common reason people stash - "I need to look at something else right now" - the better tool is `git worktree add ../hotfix -b hotfix origin/main`. That gives a second working directory with its own HEAD and index, backed by the same object database. Nothing is stashed, my build artefacts and running dev server stay intact, and switching context is a `cd`. Git refuses to check out the same branch in two worktrees, and you should remove them with `git worktree remove` rather than `rm -rf` so the administrative files get cleaned up.
