When is a WIP commit better than a stash?

flashcards.front: What are Git's four object types?
flashcards.back: Blob (raw file bytes), tree (directory listing: mode + name + object id per entry), commit (one tree + parents + author/committer + message), and annotated tag (points at an object, with tagger, message, optional signature).

flashcards.front: How is a Git object's ID computed?
flashcards.back: SHA-1 of the header plus content, where the header is the type name, a space, the content length in bytes, and a NUL byte. The result is then zlib-compressed and stored. Modern Git uses a collision-detecting SHA-1 variant (sha1dc) by default.

flashcards.front: Why does a blob not know its own filename?
flashcards.back: Names and modes live in tree entries, not blobs. That is why identical content anywhere in the repo is one object, and why Git detects renames by content similarity at diff time instead of recording them.

flashcards.front: Why does changing an old commit change every later commit ID?
flashcards.back: A commit's hash covers its tree and its parent hashes, so it transitively covers all history behind it. Change anything upstream and every descendant hash necessarily changes. This is what makes Git tamper-evident and why rebase creates new commits.

flashcards.front: What is the empty tree's object ID, and what is it for?
flashcards.back: 4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904. Use it to diff a commit against 'nothing', e.g. to list every file a root commit introduced.

flashcards.front: What is stored in .git/refs/heads/main?
flashcards.back: Forty hex characters and a newline: the object ID of the commit at the branch tip. That is all a branch is. Once there are many refs, Git compacts them into .git/packed-refs.

flashcards.front: What is HEAD?
flashcards.back: Usually a symbolic ref: the file .git/HEAD contains 'ref: refs/heads/<branch>'. git commit updates whatever ref HEAD resolves to, which is why the branch advances. If HEAD holds a raw object ID instead, you are in detached HEAD.

flashcards.front: What is detached HEAD and why is it risky?
flashcards.back: HEAD points directly at a commit rather than at a branch. You can commit, but no ref follows you, so those commits become unreachable as soon as you check out something else - recoverable only via the reflog. Bisect and CI use it deliberately.

flashcards.front: HEAD^2 vs HEAD~2?
flashcards.back: ^n selects the nth parent (only a merge commit has a second parent). ~n walks n generations back following first parents. HEAD~2 == HEAD^^.

flashcards.front: A..B vs A...B in git log?
flashcards.back: A..B = commits reachable from B but not A ('what is on my branch that is not upstream'). A...B = symmetric difference, commits unique to either side; with --left-right it gives ahead/behind counts. Note git diff A...B means something different: diff against the merge base.

flashcards.front: What determines whether an object survives garbage collection?
flashcards.back: Reachability: an object is kept if reachable from any ref, from the index, or from an unexpired reflog entry. Everything else is prunable once past the grace period.

flashcards.front: git reset --soft / --mixed / --hard: what does each touch?
flashcards.back: All move the branch pointer. --soft stops there (changes stay staged). --mixed (default) also resets the index (changes stay as unstaged edits). --hard also overwrites the working tree - the only one that destroys uncommitted work.

flashcards.front: What does `git reset <path>` (no mode flag) do?
flashcards.back: It does not move HEAD. It copies that path from HEAD into the index - i.e. unstage. Modern spelling: git restore --staged <path>.

flashcards.front: What is the index and what makes git status fast?
flashcards.back: A binary file (.git/index) with one sorted entry per tracked path: path, mode, blob ID, and a cache of the file's stat data. git status lstats files and compares stat data rather than hashing content - fast, until you have hundreds of thousands of files.

flashcards.front: What are index stages 1, 2, and 3?
flashcards.back: During a conflict the index holds three versions of the path: stage 1 = merge base, stage 2 = ours, stage 3 = theirs. `git add` collapses them into one entry, which is what marks the file resolved.

flashcards.front: What is a merge base?
flashcards.back: The best common ancestor of the two commits being merged - the third input that makes a three-way merge possible. `git merge-base A B`. There can be more than one (criss-cross history).

flashcards.front: What does the recursive/ort strategy do when there are multiple merge bases?
flashcards.back: It recursively merges the merge bases into a synthetic virtual base and three-way merges against that, instead of arbitrarily picking one ancestor.

flashcards.front: What is the default merge strategy in modern Git?
flashcards.back: ort, since Git 2.34. It replaced recursive: same idea, reimplemented on in-memory trees instead of rewriting the on-disk index, so it is much faster (especially during rebases) and fixed several rename/directory-rename bugs.

flashcards.front: -s ours vs -X ours?
flashcards.back: -X ours is an option to the normal merge: do a real merge, but resolve conflicting hunks in favour of our side. -s ours is a different strategy: produce a merge commit whose tree is exactly the current branch, discarding the other side's content entirely. Only use -s ours to retire a branch.

flashcards.front: When does a fast-forward merge happen?
flashcards.back: When the merge base equals your current commit - you have not diverged. Git just moves the branch pointer forward; no merge commit exists. --no-ff forces one anyway; --ff-only refuses to do anything else.

flashcards.front: Why does the first parent of a merge commit matter?
flashcards.back: It is the branch you were on when merging. `git log --first-parent main` therefore reads as one entry per integration, and `git revert -m 1 <merge>` means 'keep mainline, undo what came in from the side branch'.

flashcards.front: Why does rebase change commit IDs?
flashcards.back: Replayed commits get a new parent, and a commit's hash covers its parent. Author name and author date are preserved; the committer identity and committer date are new - which is how you detect a rebase after the fact.

flashcards.front: What is the golden rule of rebase, and why?
flashcards.back: Do not rebase commits others have based work on. Their clones still have the originals, so when they integrate, Git sees two lineages with the same logical changes and different IDs - and a plain `git pull` merges the old copies back in, duplicating history.

flashcards.front: git rebase --onto: argument order?
flashcards.back: git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch> - replay the commits in upstream..branch onto newbase. Used to transplant a branch started from the wrong parent, or to rescue a stacked branch whose base was squash-merged.

flashcards.front: What does `git rebase --update-refs` do?
flashcards.back: Git 2.38+. When rebasing, it also moves any other local branches that point at commits inside the rebased range, instead of leaving them on the pre-rebase copies. This is what makes stacked branches practical (rebase.updateRefs=true to default it on).

flashcards.front: How do you fold a fix into an earlier commit without a manual interactive rebase?
flashcards.back: git commit --fixup=<sha> (message becomes 'fixup! <subject>'), then git rebase -i --autosquash <base>. Git reorders it next to its target and pre-marks it fixup. Set rebase.autoSquash=true to make it default.

flashcards.front: How do you split one commit into several during an interactive rebase?
flashcards.back: Mark it `edit`. When the rebase stops: git reset HEAD^ (un-commit, keep changes in the working tree), then git add -p and commit in logical pieces, then git rebase --continue.

flashcards.front: How do you verify that every commit on a branch builds?
flashcards.back: git rebase -i --exec 'make build && make test' origin/main - inserts an exec after every commit in the range and stops at the first failure.

flashcards.front: How does cherry-pick work mechanically?
flashcards.back: It is a three-way merge with the picked commit's parent as base, the picked commit as one side, and your HEAD as the other. It can conflict; it preserves the original author but creates a new commit ID.

flashcards.front: Why always use `git cherry-pick -x`?
flashcards.back: It appends '(cherry picked from commit <sha>)' to the message. That line is the only durable link between the two copies of the change - essential when auditing months later whether a release-branch fix ever made it back to trunk.

flashcards.front: How do you check whether a fix on a release branch is also on main?
flashcards.back: git cherry -v main release/2.4 - it compares by patch-id, so it recognises cherry-picked equivalents. Lines prefixed '+' are NOT present upstream.

flashcards.front: How do you revert a merge commit, and what is the trap?
flashcards.back: git revert -m 1 <merge> keeps the first parent. The trap: the merge commit stays reachable, so Git still considers the branch merged and re-merging it later brings nothing back. Fix by reverting the revert before re-merging, or redo the work on a fresh branch.

flashcards.front: Why does rebase silently drop some commits but merge does not?
flashcards.back: Rebase compares by patch-id and skips commits whose equivalent patch is already upstream (e.g. previously cherry-picked). Merge does no such deduplication - it three-way merges, which is why duplicated cherry-picks can produce strange-looking conflicts.

flashcards.front: What is `git rerere` and what is its failure mode?
flashcards.back: REuse REcorded REsolution: records how you resolved each conflicted hunk and replays it automatically when the identical conflict recurs. Invaluable during long rebases. Failure mode: it silently replays a WRONG resolution forever - use `git rerere forget <path>` to clear it.

flashcards.front: What does merge.conflictStyle=diff3 (or zdiff3) give you?
flashcards.back: It adds the merge base between ||||||| and ======= markers, so you can see what each side changed rather than only what each side has. zdiff3 (2.35+) is the same but hoists common leading/trailing lines out of the conflict block.

flashcards.front: Why are 'ours' and 'theirs' inverted during a rebase?
flashcards.back: Rebase checks out the upstream and replays your commits onto it, so ours = the branch you are rebasing onto and theirs = your own commit being replayed. Blindly taking --ours during a rebase discards your work.

flashcards.front: How do you stop package-lock.json from ever auto-merging?
flashcards.back: In .gitattributes: `package-lock.json -merge`. Git then always reports a conflict instead of interleaving two machine-generated files, and you resolve by regenerating the file.

flashcards.front: What is the reflog and where does it live?
flashcards.back: A per-ref, local, append-only log of every value that ref has held: .git/logs/HEAD and .git/logs/refs/heads/*. Never pushed, never fetched, absent from a fresh clone.

flashcards.front: Reflog expiry defaults?
flashcards.back: gc.reflogExpire = 90 days for entries reachable from the ref tip; gc.reflogExpireUnreachable = 30 days for the rest. Unreachable loose objects are pruned only when older than gc.pruneExpire, default 2 weeks.

flashcards.front: What can the reflog NOT recover?
flashcards.back: Anything never written to the object database: uncommitted, unstaged edits destroyed by reset --hard; untracked files removed by git clean -fdx; ignored files. Also anything on someone else's machine, and anything past reflog expiry plus gc.

flashcards.front: You ran a bad `git reset --hard`. First command?
flashcards.back: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD (reset/merge/rebase/pull all write it), or git reset --hard HEAD@{1} from the reflog. The commits were unreferenced, not deleted.

flashcards.front: How do you recover a stash you dropped?
flashcards.back: Stash entries are commits, so: git fsck --unreachable | grep commit, then git log -1 on the candidates looking for a 'WIP on ...' subject, then git stash apply <sha>. Works until gc prunes them.

flashcards.front: git bisect run exit codes?
flashcards.back: 0 = good/old. 1-127 except 125 = bad/new. 125 = untestable, skip this commit. 128-255 = abort the bisect. Returning 125 for commits that do not build is what keeps an automated bisect honest.

flashcards.front: How do you make git bisect survive a flaky test?
flashcards.back: Make the reproducer deterministic if you can; otherwise run it N times in the script and only report good if all N pass. Biasing toward 'bad' is safer - a false good prunes the half containing the real culprit.

flashcards.front: What does `git bisect --first-parent` do?
flashcards.back: Restricts the search to the mainline, never descending into feature branches. On a merge-based main it avoids half-finished commits that do not build and blames the merge - which is usually the unit that actually shipped.

flashcards.front: What does `git stash push -u` change?
flashcards.back: It also stashes untracked files (as a third parent commit). Without it, `git stash` followed by `git clean -fd` permanently deletes untracked work, because it was never in the object database.

flashcards.front: What is a git worktree?
flashcards.back: A second working directory with its own HEAD and index, sharing the same object database: git worktree add ../hotfix -b hotfix origin/main. Better than stashing for context switches - your build artefacts survive. The same branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees.

flashcards.front: What is a remote-tracking branch?
flashcards.back: A local cache of a remote ref, under refs/remotes/origin/*, updated by git fetch via the refspec +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*. origin/main means 'main as of my last fetch', not 'main right now'.

flashcards.front: --force-with-lease vs --force-if-includes?
flashcards.back: --force-with-lease rejects the push if the remote ref differs from your remote-tracking ref - but any background fetch updates that ref and silently disarms it. --force-if-includes (2.30+) additionally requires the remote tip be reachable from your reflog, proving you actually integrated it.

flashcards.front: Why is `pull.ff = only` a good default?
flashcards.back: A pull then either fast-forwards or stops and tells you the branches diverged, instead of silently creating a 'Merge branch main of ...' commit. You then choose rebase or merge deliberately.

flashcards.front: Why can't client-side hooks enforce policy?
flashcards.back: git commit --no-verify and git push --no-verify skip them, and anyone can delete the file in .git/hooks. They are fast feedback. Real enforcement is a pre-receive hook (self-hosted) or branch protection plus required status checks (SaaS).

flashcards.front: How do you distribute hooks to a team?
flashcards.back: .git/hooks is not cloned, so commit a directory such as .githooks/ and set core.hooksPath to it (Git 2.9+), or use husky / lefthook / the pre-commit framework to install it automatically.

flashcards.front: pre-receive vs update vs post-receive?
flashcards.back: pre-receive runs once with all ref updates on stdin; non-zero rejects the entire push atomically. update runs once per ref, so it can reject some refs and accept others. post-receive runs after acceptance - notifications, CI triggers, deploys.

flashcards.front: What is a submodule, at the object level?
flashcards.back: A tree entry with mode 160000 (a gitlink) whose object ID is a commit SHA belonging to another repository, plus a tracked .gitmodules file mapping that path to a URL. The superproject stores only the pin.

flashcards.front: The most common submodule outage?
flashcards.back: Pushing the superproject without pushing the submodule first. Everyone else gets a gitlink pointing at a commit that does not exist on the remote: 'fatal: reference is not a tree'. Fix: push the child first, or git push --recurse-submodules=on-demand, plus push.recurseSubmodules=check.

flashcards.front: Submodule vs subtree, in one line each?
flashcards.back: Submodule: a pinned pointer to another repo - exact, auditable, but needs init, has detached HEAD, and needs credentials for the child. Subtree: the content is copied into your tree - a plain clone just works, but the repo grows and pushing changes upstream is clunky.

flashcards.front: Why does `git branch --merged` miss squash-merged branches?
flashcards.back: It works by reachability. A squash-merge creates a NEW commit with the same content but a different ID, so the branch's own commits were never merged into main. Use `git cherry` (patch-id based) or the platform's PR state instead.

flashcards.front: What problem does a merge queue solve?
flashcards.back: Semantic conflicts: two PRs each green against main can break main when combined (one renames a function, the other adds a caller). A merge queue builds and tests the prospective merged result in order and only fast-forwards main if it passes.

flashcards.front: Trunk-based development in one sentence?
flashcards.back: Everyone integrates into one trunk at least daily, branches live hours not weeks, incomplete work ships disabled behind feature flags, and release branches are stabilisation-only with fixes cherry-picked from trunk.

flashcards.front: Why fix on trunk first and cherry-pick to release branches, not the reverse?
flashcards.back: If you fix on the release branch and rely on merging it forward later, a missed merge silently reships the bug in the next release. Trunk-first makes it impossible for the fix to be lost.

flashcards.front: Partial clone filters: blob:none vs tree:0 vs --depth=1?
flashcards.back: --filter=blob:none keeps the full commit graph and fetches file contents on demand (history, merge-base and blame still work). --filter=tree:0 also omits trees - smallest, but most history traversal needs the network. --depth=1 truncates history and breaks describe, merge-base, and blame.

flashcards.front: What does sparse-checkout cone mode buy you?
flashcards.back: Patterns are restricted to whole directories, so Git uses fast prefix matching instead of per-path gitignore-style evaluation, and it enables the sparse index - an excluded directory becomes one index entry instead of thousands, which is what actually makes git status fast.

flashcards.front: How does Git LFS work?
flashcards.back: A clean/smudge filter configured via .gitattributes. The committed content is a small text pointer (version, sha256 oid, size); the real bytes live on an LFS server and are fetched on checkout. Adopt it before the binaries land - retrofitting requires a history rewrite.

flashcards.front: What is a packfile and how does it save space?
flashcards.back: A single .pack file (plus .idx) holding many objects, where similar objects are stored as deltas against each other within a sliding window (pack.window=10, pack.depth=50) and then zlib-compressed. Deltas are a storage detail; the object model is still snapshots.

flashcards.front: What does the commit-graph file do?
flashcards.back: Caches commit metadata plus generation numbers (a topological level per commit) so merge-base, ancestry checks, and log --graph can prune the walk instead of traversing all history. Maintained automatically since Git 2.24 and by `git maintenance`.

flashcards.front: Lightweight vs annotated tag?
flashcards.back: Lightweight is just a ref under refs/tags pointing at a commit. Annotated creates a real tag object with a tagger, date, message, and optional signature, and the ref points at that. Use annotated for anything published.

flashcards.front: Why must you never move a published tag?
flashcards.back: Clients do not update tags they already have by default, so v1.4.0 would mean different commits on different machines - the worst possible property for a release identifier. Ship v1.4.1 instead.

flashcards.front: What does `git describe --contains <sha>` tell you?
flashcards.back: The first tag that contains that commit - i.e. which release shipped it. The forward direction, `git describe --tags`, yields strings like v1.4.0-17-g9f3c1ab, which is what you should embed in your binary's version output.

flashcards.front: What does a commit signature actually prove?
flashcards.back: That the holder of a key produced that object and that its content, including all history behind it, is unmodified. It does not prove the code is good, and it proves nothing unless someone verifies it - so enforce 'require signed commits' at the platform. Web-UI merges are signed by the platform, not the author.

flashcards.front: First step when a secret is pushed to a repository?
flashcards.back: Rotate the credential. Removing it from history is cleanup; revocation is the only containment. Assume compromise the moment it reached a shared remote - public repos are scraped within minutes.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't `git rm secrets.env` remove the secret?
flashcards.back: It only changes the current tree. The blob is still reachable from every historical commit that contained it, so `git show <old-sha>:secrets.env` still works. Removal requires rewriting every commit from the introducing one forward - which changes every descendant hash.

flashcards.front: Which tool rewrites history to purge a file, and why not filter-branch?
flashcards.back: git filter-repo (Git's own docs recommend it) or BFG for simple cases. filter-branch is very slow and has many correctness footguns, and now prints a warning steering you to filter-repo.

flashcards.front: After a history rewrite, why might the secret still be reachable on GitHub?
flashcards.back: Forks retain the old objects and share an object store with upstream, so the commit is often still fetchable by SHA; refs/pull/<n>/head keeps PR heads alive; and the server only truly drops them when it garbage-collects, which usually needs a support request.

flashcards.front: git log -S vs git log -G?
flashcards.back: -S finds commits where the NUMBER of occurrences of the string changed - i.e. it was introduced or removed. -G finds commits whose diff text matches the regex at all, including modifications and moves that leave the count unchanged.

flashcards.front: How do you stop a bulk reformat commit from ruining git blame?
flashcards.back: Put its SHA in a committed .git-blame-ignore-revs file and set blame.ignoreRevsFile to it (or pass --ignore-rev). GitHub's web blame honours the file too. Also use blame -w -C -C -C.

flashcards.front: What does `git log -L 40,80:file.go` do?
flashcards.back: Shows the complete evolution of that line range, commit by commit with diffs, following the range as it moves. `-L :funcName:file.go` does the same for a function. Better than blame when the question is 'why is this like this'.

flashcards.front: Why might a commit's author date and committer date differ?
flashcards.back: It was rebased, cherry-picked, or amended - those preserve the author date but set a new committer date. Important during incidents: the commit date is not the deploy time, and a commit can appear in main long after it was written.

flashcards.front: How do you fetch a GitHub pull request that isn't a branch?
flashcards.back: GitHub exposes PRs as refs/pull/<n>/head (and /merge). Fetch them explicitly, e.g. git fetch origin 'refs/pull/*/head:refs/remotes/origin/pr/*', or git fetch origin pull/1234/head:pr-1234.

flashcards.front: --assume-unchanged vs --skip-worktree?
flashcards.back: Both stop Git noticing local edits. --assume-unchanged is a performance promise Git may ignore; --skip-worktree is honoured more strongly and is what sparse-checkout uses. Neither is a supported way to keep local config edits out of commits - they cause silently-lost changes.

flashcards.front: What does `git maintenance` do that `git gc` doesn't?
flashcards.back: Git 2.29+. It can be scheduled in the background and runs incremental tasks - incremental repack, commit-graph write, multi-pack-index, prefetch - avoiding the long stop-the-world repack that a full gc performs.

flashcards.front: Is `git gc --aggressive` a good routine?
flashcards.back: No. It discards existing deltas and recomputes them with a much larger window and depth - expensive, and it throws away good delta chains from previous packs. Worth trying once on a badly-packed repo; not a maintenance habit.
